title: Fizz Buzz
statement: Count from 1 to n and return a list of n strings. For a multiple of 3 the entry is "Tick", for a multiple of 5 it is "Tock", for a multiple of both it is "TickTock", and otherwise it is the number itself written as a string (for example "7").
hint: Check divisibility by 15 (or build the string from both checks) before checking 3 or 5 alone.

title: Running Sum of 1d Array
statement:
Given the array nums, return its running (prefix) sum: an array of the same length whose i-th value is nums[0] + nums[1] + … + nums[i].

The totals can be larger than an int, so return an array of long.
hint: Keep one running total and add each element to it. The total can exceed int, so use long in Java.

title: Richest Customer Wealth
statement: The grid sales has one row per shop, and sales[i][j] is what shop i sold on day j. A shop's total is the sum of its row. Return the largest total among all shops.
hint: Sum each row in an inner loop and keep the best total seen so far.

title: Number of Steps to Reduce a Number to Zero
statement:
Start with the number n. In one move, if the number is even divide it by 2, otherwise subtract 1. Return how many moves it takes to reach 0.

n can be larger than an int, so it is passed as a long.
hint: Just simulate with a while loop. Use long in Java.

title: Count the Digits That Divide a Number
statement: Given a positive integer n, return how many of its digits divide n exactly. Count a repeated digit each time it appears, and skip zeros.
hint: Peel digits with % 10 on a copy of n, and test n % digit == 0 on the original.

title: Palindrome Number
statement: Return true if the integer n reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise false. Negative numbers are never mirrors (the minus sign would end up on the wrong side).
hint: Reverse the number with rev = rev * 10 + n % 10 and compare it with the original. Try it without converting to a string.

title: Plus One
statement:
A large number is given as the array digits, most significant digit first. Add 1 to the number and return the digits of the result in the same format.

The number has no leading zero unless it is 0 itself.
hint: Walk from the last digit. A 9 becomes 0 and carries; any other digit just goes up by one and you stop. If every digit was 9, put a 1 in front.

title: Reverse Integer
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return the number with its digits reversed. Leading zeros in the result are dropped (so 1200 becomes 21).
hint: Build the answer as rev = rev * 10 + n % 10 while n > 0.

title: Sum of Digits
statement:
Given a non-negative integer n, return the sum of its digits.

n can be larger than an int, so it is passed as a long.
hint: Repeatedly take n % 10 to get the last digit, then do n / 10. Use long in Java.

title: Prime or Not
statement: Return true if the integer n is prime, otherwise false. A prime has exactly two divisors, 1 and itself, so 1 is not prime.
hint: You only need to try divisors up to √n. Remember 1 is not prime.

title: GCD and LCM
statement:
Given two positive integers a and b, return an array of two values: [gcd, lcm], their greatest common divisor followed by their least common multiple.

The LCM can be much larger than an int, so the result is an array of long.
hint: Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b). Then lcm = a / gcd * b, which needs long in Java.

title: Find Numbers with Even Number of Digits
statement:
You are given an array nums of positive integers. Return how many of them have an even number of digits.

For example, 7896 has 4 digits (even) and 345 has 3 digits (odd).
hint: Count digits by dividing by 10 until the number is 0, then check the count is even.

title: Remove Element
statement:
Remove every occurrence of val from nums, keeping the other elements in their original order. Return the remaining elements as an array (an empty array if nothing remains).

Try doing it in place with one write pointer, then return the first k elements.
hint: Keep w = 0. For each element not equal to V, copy it to a[w] and increase w.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
statement:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. Keep only the first copy of each value and return the distinct values, in order, as an array.

Try doing it in place with a write pointer, then return the first k elements.
hint: Because equal values sit together, compare each element with the last one you kept.

title: Merge Sorted Array
statement: Arrays x and y are each sorted in non-decreasing order. Return one sorted array containing all their values, built in a single pass without calling a sort function.
hint: Two pointers i and j: always take the smaller of x[i] and y[j], then copy whatever is left.

title: Check if Array Is Sorted and Rotated
statement:
Return true if nums could be a non-decreasing array that was rotated some number of positions (zero rotations counts too), otherwise return false.

For example, [3, 4, 5, 1, 2] is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] rotated, so the answer is true.
hint: Count places where a[i] > a[(i+1) % N], wrapping around. A rotated sorted array has at most one such drop.

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
statement:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain negatives. Return a new array with the squares of all elements, sorted in non-decreasing order.

Can you do it in O(n) without sorting again?
hint: The largest square is at one of the two ends. Use two pointers and fill the answer from the back.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement: prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may buy on one day and sell on a later day. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no trade makes money.
hint: Track the cheapest price so far. Each day, the best sale today is price minus that minimum.

title: Rotate Array
statement:
Rotate the array nums to the right by k steps, in place. Your function returns nothing; we check nums afterwards.

Rotating [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] right by 2 gives [4, 5, 1, 2, 3].
hint: Rotating by N changes nothing, so use K % N. Element i moves to (i + K) % N.

title: Second Largest Element
statement:
Return the second largest distinct value in nums. If it does not exist (all values are equal), return -1.

For example, in [4, 9, 2, 9, 7] the largest is 9 and the second largest distinct value is 7.
hint: One pass: keep first and second. When you see a bigger value, the old first becomes second. Skip values equal to first.

title: Move Zeros to End
statement: Move all zeros in nums to the end while keeping the order of the non-zero elements. Do it in place: your function returns nothing and we check nums afterwards.
hint: Keep a pointer w for the next write position. Copy each non-zero to a[w++], then fill the rest with zeros.

title: Two Sum
statement: Return true if there are two different positions i ≠ j with nums[i] + nums[j] == target, otherwise return false.
hint: Walk the array once. Before adding x to a set, check whether T − x is already in it.

title: Contains Duplicate
statement: Return true if some value appears at least twice in nums, otherwise return false.
hint: Add values to a HashSet as you go; if one is already there, you found a repeat.

title: Valid Anagram
statement: You are given two lowercase words a and b. Return true if one is a rearrangement of the other (the same letters with the same counts), otherwise return false.
hint: Use an int[26] array: add counts for the first word, subtract for the second, and check everything is zero.

title: Ransom Note
statement: You want to spell note by cutting letters out of magazine. Each magazine letter can be used only once. Return true if the note can be built, otherwise false.
hint: Count the magazine's letters, then spend one count for each letter of the note. If a count goes below zero, it's impossible.

title: First Unique Character in a String
statement: Given a lowercase string s, return the 0-based index of the first character that appears exactly once in s. If there is no such character, return -1.
hint: First pass: count every letter in an array of 26. Second pass: return the first index whose count is 1.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays
statement: Given two integer arrays a and b, return every distinct value that appears in both, in increasing order. If they share no value, return an empty list.
hint: Put the first array in a set, then collect values of the second that are in it (into another set to avoid duplicates), and sort.

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Given a list of lowercase words, group together the words made of exactly the same letters. Return the groups as a list of lists: sort the words inside each group alphabetically (keep duplicates), and order the groups by comparing them word by word (alphabetically, like sorting lists).
hint: The sorted letters of a word are its key, e.g. eat → aet. Map key → list of words, then sort each list and the list of groups.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
statement: The array nums is unsorted. Return the length of the longest set of values x, x+1, x+2, … that are all present in nums. Aim for O(n).
hint: Put everything in a set. Only start counting from x when x − 1 is not in the set, so each run is walked once.

title: Most Frequent Element
statement: Return the value that appears most often in nums. If several values tie for the highest count, return the smallest of them.
hint: Count with a HashMap / dict, then scan the counts for the best (value, count) pair.

title: Height Checker
statement: Students should stand in non-decreasing order of height. Given the current line heights, return how many positions hold a different height from the correctly sorted line.
hint: Make a sorted copy and compare position by position. With heights ≤ 100, counting sort works too.

title: Relative Sort Array
statement: Array order has distinct values and defines an ordering. Return array a rearranged so that values appearing in order come first, in the same order as in order. Values of a not in order go at the end in increasing order.
hint: Map each value of order to its index, then sort a with a comparator: known values by index, unknown values after them by value.

title: Largest Perimeter Triangle
statement: Choose three of the stick lengths in sticks to form a triangle with positive area (each side shorter than the other two combined). Return the largest possible perimeter, or 0 if no triangle can be formed.
hint: Sort descending. For the longest side a[i], the best partners are the next two; check a[i] < a[i+1] + a[i+2].

title: Sort an Array
statement:
You are given an integer array nums. Return the same values in non-decreasing order.

Try writing a simple sort yourself first (bubble, selection or insertion), then compare with the built-in sort: the simple O(n²) sorts are fine for small arrays but will run out of time on the largest tests, so finish with an O(n log n) sort.
hint: Insertion sort: take each element and shift bigger elements one step right until you find its place.

title: H-Index
statement: An author's papers have the citation counts given in citations. Their score is the largest h such that at least h papers have h or more citations each. Return h.
hint: Sort in descending order. The paper at index i (0-based) supports h = i + 1 if it has at least i + 1 citations.

title: K-th Smallest
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k-th smallest element (counting duplicates, 1-based).
hint: Sort, then the answer sits at index K − 1.

title: Matrix Diagonal Sum
statement: Given a square matrix mat (n × n), return the sum of both diagonals. If n is odd, count the centre cell only once.
hint: Main diagonal is [i][i], the other is [i][N−1−i]. Subtract the centre once when N is odd.

title: Transpose Matrix
statement: Given a rows × cols matrix matrix, return its transpose: row i of the answer is column i of the input, so the answer has cols rows and rows columns.
hint: Answer cell [j][i] = input cell [i][j]. Loop j on the outside when printing.

title: Reshape the Matrix
statement:
Read the grid grid row by row and refill a new grid with newRows rows and newCols columns in the same row-by-row order. Return the new grid.

If the new size does not hold the same number of cells as grid, return grid unchanged.
hint: Cell number k in reading order lives at (k / C, k % C) in the old grid and goes to (k / NC, k % NC) in the new one.

title: Rotate Image
statement: Rotate the square grid grid (n × n) 90° clockwise in place. Your function returns nothing; we check grid afterwards.
hint: Clockwise rotation = transpose (swap m[i][j] and m[j][i]), then reverse each row.

title: Spiral Matrix
statement: Given a rows × cols matrix matrix, return all of its cells in clockwise spiral order, starting from the top-left.
hint: Keep four walls: top, bottom, left, right. Walk one edge, then move that wall inward. Check the walls haven't crossed before the bottom and left edges.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
statement: For every cell of grid that is 0 in the original grid, set its whole row and whole column to 0. Change grid in place; your function returns nothing and we check grid afterwards.
hint: First record which rows and which columns contain a zero, then do a second pass to write zeros. Don't zero while you're still scanning.

title: Valid Sudoku
statement: A partly filled 9 × 9 Sudoku grid board uses the characters '1'–'9' and '.' for empty cells. Return true if no row, column or 3 × 3 box contains the same digit twice, otherwise false. You don't need to check whether it can be solved.
hint: Use 27 sets (or boolean arrays): one per row, column and box. Box index is (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
statement:
Each row of grid is sorted left to right, and the first value of each row is larger than the last value of the row above. For every value in queries, decide whether it appears in the grid.

Return a list of booleans, one per query in the same order (true = present). Aim for O(log(rows·cols)) per query.
hint: Read the grid as one sorted array of length R·C. Index k is cell (k / C, k % C), so plain binary search works.

title: Move Zeroes
statement: A shelf of boxes is described by nums; a 0 means an empty slot. Rearrange nums in place so every non-zero value keeps its original relative order and all zeros end up at the end. Return nothing; we inspect nums afterwards.
hint: Keep a write pointer for the next non-zero spot; copy non-zeros forward, then fill the tail with zeros.

title: Two Sum II
statement: The prices in nums are sorted in non-decreasing order. Find two different positions whose values add up to target and return their 1-based positions [i, j] with i < j. Exactly one such pair exists. Use only O(1) extra space.
hint: Put one pointer at each end: a sum that is too small moves the left pointer right, too large moves the right pointer left.

title: 3Sum
statement:
Given nums, return every distinct trio of values [a, b, c] taken from three different positions such that a + b + c = 0. Two trios are the same if they contain the same values. Return each trio in any order, and the trios in any order.

Example: in [3,-1,-2,0,1] the trios are [-2,-1,3] and [-1,0,1].
hint: Sort, fix the first value, then use two pointers on the rest; skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicates.

title: Sort Colors
statement: Each entry of flags is 0, 1 or 2 (three colours). Rearrange the array in place so all 0s come first, then all 1s, then all 2s, without calling a library sort. Return nothing; we inspect flags afterwards.
hint: Dutch national flag: keep low, mid and high pointers; swap 0s to low, 2s to high, and step over 1s.

title: Container With Most Water
statement: Vertical walls stand at positions 0..n-1; wall i has height walls[i]. Choosing two walls i < j forms a tank that holds (j - i) × min(walls[i], walls[j]) units of water (the walls in between are ignored). Return the largest amount any tank can hold.
hint: Start with the widest pair and always move the shorter wall inward, since keeping it can never give a larger tank.

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement:
heights[i] is the height of a 1-unit-wide column. After a heavy rain, water settles on top of columns wherever it is held in by taller columns on both sides. Return the total units of water trapped.

Above column i, the water level is min(tallest to its left, tallest to its right), counting itself.
hint: Move two pointers inward from the ends, always advancing the side with the smaller running maximum and adding (that max − height).

title: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K
statement: Consider every block of exactly k consecutive elements of nums in which no value appears twice. Return the largest sum among those blocks, or 0 if no such block exists.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ nums.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, every window sum fits in a 32-bit integer
hint: Slide a window of size k, keeping a running sum and a count map; a window qualifies when the map has k keys.

title: Max Consecutive Ones
statement: A row of lamps is given as lamps, where 1 means on and 0 means off. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive lamps that are all on.
hint: Walk once, growing a counter on 1s and resetting it on 0s; track the maximum.

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
statement: lamps holds 1 (working) and 0 (broken) lamps in a row. You may repair at most k broken lamps, turning them into 1s. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive working lamps you can achieve.
hint: Keep the longest window containing at most k zeros; shrink from the left whenever the zero count exceeds k.

title: Subarray Product Less Than K
statement: Given positive integers nums and a cap k, count the contiguous non-empty subarrays whose product of all elements is strictly less than k.
constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 1000, 0 ≤ k ≤ 10<sup>6</sup>, the answer fits in a 32-bit integer
hint: Grow the right end, divide out from the left while the product ≥ k; each right end adds (window length) subarrays.

title: Fruits Into Baskets
statement: Trees stand in a row and trees[i] is the fruit type of tree i. You carry two bags, each of which may hold only one fruit type (unlimited amount). Starting at any tree, you pick one fruit from every tree while walking right and must stop at the first tree whose fruit fits neither bag. Return the maximum number of fruits you can collect.
hint: Find the longest window containing at most two distinct values, using a count map and a moving left edge.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
statement: Given positive integers nums and a goal, return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least goal. Return 0 if no subarray reaches it.
hint: Expand the right end; while the window sum reaches the goal, record its length and shrink from the left.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
statement: A frame of width k slides over readings from left to right, one step at a time. For every position of the frame, record the largest reading inside it. Return the list of these maxima (it has n - k + 1 entries).
hint: Keep a deque of indices whose values are decreasing; pop smaller values from the back and expired indices from the front.

title: Subarray with K Distinct Integers
statement:
Count the contiguous subarrays of nums that contain exactly k different values.

For instance, [1,2,1] has exactly 2 different values, while [1,1] has 1.
constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, 1 ≤ nums[i], k ≤ nums.length, the answer fits in a 32-bit integer
hint: exactly(k) = atMost(k) − atMost(k−1), and atMost is a classic shrinking window with a count map.

title: Find Pivot Index
statement: A seesaw has weights w placed in a row. Index i is a balance point if the sum of weights strictly to its left equals the sum strictly to its right (an empty side sums to 0). Return the leftmost balance point, or -1 if there is none.
hint: With the total known, the right sum at i is total − left − w[i]; scan once keeping the left sum.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
statement: Count how many contiguous non-empty subarrays of nums sum to exactly k. Values may be negative.
hint: Count prefix sums in a map; at each prefix p, add how many earlier prefixes equal p − k.

title: Matrix Block Sum
statement: Given an m × n grid grid and a radius k, build a grid of the same size where cell (r, c) holds the sum of every grid[i][j] with |i − r| ≤ k and |j − c| ≤ k (cells outside the grid are ignored). Return the new grid.
hint: Build a 2-D prefix sum once; each answer is a rectangle sum with clamped corners.

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: For each index i of nums, compute the product of all elements except nums[i]. Return these products as an array. Do it in O(n) time without using division. Every such product fits in a 32-bit integer.
hint: out[i] = (product of everything left of i) × (product of everything right of i); fill with two passes.

title: Continuous Subarray Sum
statement: Given non-negative integers nums and a positive integer k, return true if there is a contiguous subarray of length at least 2 whose sum is a multiple of k (0 counts as a multiple), otherwise false.
hint: Two prefixes with the same remainder mod k bound a multiple of k; store the earliest index per remainder and require a gap of 2.

title: Subarray Sum Divisible by K
statement: Count the contiguous non-empty subarrays of nums whose sum is divisible by k. Values may be negative; a sum of 0 counts.
constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, −10<sup>4</sup> ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>, 2 ≤ k ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>, the answer fits in a 32-bit integer
hint: Count prefix remainders (normalised to be non-negative); pairs with equal remainder give valid subarrays.

title: Maximum Subarray
statement: profit[i] is a shop's profit (possibly negative) on day i. Choose a non-empty stretch of consecutive days and return the largest total profit any stretch can have.
hint: Kadane: the best stretch ending today is either today alone or today plus the best stretch ending yesterday.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
statement: Return the largest product obtainable from a non-empty contiguous subarray of nums. Values can be negative or zero. Every product involved fits in a 32-bit integer.
hint: Track both the largest and the smallest product ending here, because a negative number swaps them.

title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
statement: The numbers in ring are arranged in a circle, so the element after the last one is the first. Pick a non-empty stretch of consecutive elements (it may wrap around, but may use each element at most once) and return the largest possible sum.
constraints: 1 ≤ ring.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, −3·10<sup>4</sup> ≤ ring[i] ≤ 3·10<sup>4</sup>, the sum of all |ring[i]| is below 2<sup>31</sup>
hint: Answer = max(normal Kadane max, total − Kadane min), except when every value is negative, where only the first applies.

title: Maximum Absolute Sum of Any Subarray
statement: moves[i] is a daily change (up or down). The swing of a stretch of consecutive days is the absolute value of its total. Return the largest swing over all stretches; an empty stretch has swing 0.
hint: Run Kadane twice (for the largest and the most negative sum), or take max prefix − min prefix.

title: Reverse a String
statement: You are given a word as an array of characters letters. Reverse the order of the characters in place using O(1) extra memory. Return nothing; we inspect letters afterwards.
hint: Swap the outermost pair and move both pointers inward until they meet.

title: Valid Palindrome
statement: Return true if the phrase s reads the same forwards and backwards once you drop every character that is not a letter or digit and ignore upper/lower case; otherwise return false. A phrase with nothing left after cleaning counts as true.
hint: Two pointers from both ends: skip non-alphanumerics, compare lower-cased characters.

title: Valid Palindrome II
statement: You hold an eraser that can remove at most one character from the lowercase string s. Return true if s can be made into a palindrome this way (or already is one), otherwise false.
hint: Compare from both ends; at the first mismatch, check whether skipping the left or the right character leaves a palindrome.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
statement: Return the longest contiguous piece of s that reads the same forwards and backwards. If several pieces share the maximum length, return the one that starts earliest (leftmost).
hint: Expand around each of the 2n−1 centres (characters and gaps between them) and keep the longest.

title: Palindromic Substrings
statement: Count how many contiguous non-empty pieces of s read the same forwards and backwards. Pieces at different positions are counted separately even if their text is equal (so "aa" contains 3).
hint: Expand around every centre and add one for each successful expansion step.

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
statement: Find every starting index i in text such that the piece of length |word| starting at i is a rearrangement of word (same letters, same counts). Return the indices in increasing order.
hint: Slide a window of length |word| over text with a 26-letter count array and compare it with word's counts.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Return the length of the longest contiguous piece of s in which no character appears more than once. The empty string has answer 0.
constraints: 0 ≤ s.length ≤ 5·10<sup>4</sup>, printable ASCII (letters, digits, symbols, spaces)
hint: Remember the last index of each character; when a repeat appears inside the window, jump the left edge past it.

title: Permutation in String
statement: Return true if some contiguous piece of message is a rearrangement of code (uses exactly the same letters with the same counts), otherwise false.
hint: Slide a window of length |code| across message, maintaining letter counts, and check for a match at each step.

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement: Return the shortest contiguous piece of s that contains every character of need, counting repeats (if need has two as, the piece needs at least two). If several shortest pieces exist, return the one starting earliest. If none exists, return the empty string.
constraints: 1 ≤ s.length, need.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, upper and lower case letters (case-sensitive)
hint: Expand the right edge until all counts are covered, then shrink the left edge as far as possible, recording the best window.

title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
statement: All strings in words have the same length. A glued block is any string formed by joining every word of words exactly once, in some order (duplicates in the list must be used as many times as they appear). Return all starting indices in s where a glued block begins, in increasing order.
hint: For each offset modulo the word length, slide a window word-by-word with a count map, shrinking when a word is over-used.

title: Majority Element
statement:
Each entry of votes is a candidate number. One candidate received more than half of all votes. Return that candidate.

Bonus: solve it in O(1) extra space.
constraints: 1 ≤ votes.length ≤ 5·10<sup>4</sup>, −10<sup>9</sup> ≤ votes[i] ≤ 10<sup>9</sup>, a majority always exists
hint: Count frequencies with a map, or use Boyer–Moore voting: matching votes add one, others cancel one.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: Return the k values that occur most often in nums, ordered from most to least frequent. When two values occur equally often, the smaller value comes first (this tie rule also decides who makes the cut).
constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, 1 ≤ k ≤ number of distinct values
hint: Count with a hash map, then sort the distinct values by (−count, value), or bucket by count.

title: Sort Characters By Frequency
statement: Rearrange the characters of s so that more frequent characters come first, with all copies of a character kept together. If two characters occur equally often, the one with the smaller character code comes first (so 'A' before 'a', digits before letters). Return the new string.
constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 5·10<sup>5</sup>, upper/lower case letters and digits
hint: Count each character, sort the distinct characters by (−count, character), then repeat each one count times.

title: Binary Search
statement:
A gym keeps its locker numbers in a list nums sorted in increasing order, with no repeats. Given a locker number target, return its position (0-based) in the list, or -1 if it is not there.

Aim for O(log n) time.
hint: Keep a window [lo, hi]. Compare the middle value to target and throw away the half that cannot contain it.

title: Sqrt(x)
statement:
Given a non-negative integer x, return the largest integer r such that r * r ≤ x (the square root rounded down). Do not use a built-in square root or power function.

For example, for x = 20 the answer is 4 because 4·4 = 16 ≤ 20 but 5·5 = 25 > 20.
hint: Binary search r in [0, x]: if mid·mid ≤ x, mid is a candidate and you search higher; otherwise search lower. Watch for overflow — use 64-bit math.

title: Search Insert Position
statement:
Books on a shelf are labelled with distinct numbers stored in increasing order in nums. Return the index of target if it is on the shelf; otherwise return the index where it would be placed to keep the shelf sorted.

Aim for O(log n) time.
hint: You want the first index whose value is ≥ target (a lower bound). Binary search for it; if none exists the answer is n.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
statement:
A list of distinct numbers was sorted in increasing order and then rotated: some prefix was cut off and moved to the end (the rotation may be zero). Given this list nums and a value target, return the index of target, or -1 if it is absent.

Your solution should run in O(log n).
hint: At every mid, one of the halves [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] is normally sorted. Check whether target lies inside that sorted half to decide where to go.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: The list nums holds distinct numbers that were sorted in increasing order and then rotated by an unknown amount (possibly zero). Return the smallest value in the list in O(log n) time.
hint: Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]: if it is larger, the minimum lies strictly to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left.

title: Find Peak Element
statement:
A hiking trail's elevations are recorded in heights. The trail climbs strictly, reaches a single summit, and then descends strictly (either the climb or the descent may be empty). Return the index of the summit, i.e. the unique position whose value is larger than both neighbours (positions outside the array count as −∞).

Solve it in O(log n) time.
constraints: 1 ≤ heights.length ≤ 2000, adjacent values differ, exactly one summit
hint: Look at heights[mid] and heights[mid+1]: if the trail is still going up, the summit is to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left.

title: Find First and Last Position of Element
statement:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain repeats. Return [first, last]: the first and last index where target appears. If it does not appear, return [-1, -1].

Use O(log n) time.
hint: Run two binary searches: one for the first index with value ≥ target and one for the first index with value > target.

title: Search a 2D Matrix II
statement: In the grid matrix, every row increases from left to right and every column increases from top to bottom. Return true if target appears somewhere in the grid and false otherwise.
hint: Start at the top-right corner. If the value is too big move left, if too small move down — each step removes a whole row or column.

title: Koko Eating Bananas
statement: A hamster has jars of seeds; jar i holds piles[i] seeds. It picks a fixed pace of s seeds per hour. Each hour it eats up to s seeds from one jar (if the jar has fewer left, it finishes the jar and waits for the rest of the hour). Return the smallest integer pace s that lets it empty all jars within h hours.
hint: The hours needed shrink as s grows. Binary search s in [1, max(piles)], computing hours as the sum of ceil(pile / s).

title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
statement: Crates with weights weights wait on a dock in a fixed order. A ferry makes one trip per day and loads crates in order until the next crate would exceed its load limit. Return the smallest load limit that gets every crate across in at most days trips.
hint: The answer lies between max(weights) and sum(weights). For a candidate limit, greedily count the trips needed and binary search on that.

title: Min Speed to Arrive on Time
statement:
You ride a chain of buses; bus i covers dist[i] km, and all buses travel at the same integer speed you choose. Buses only depart on the hour, so after every ride except the last you wait until the next whole hour. Return the smallest integer speed (km/h) that gets you to the end within hour hours, or -1 if no speed up to 107 works.

hour has at most two digits after the decimal point.
hint: Time at speed s is sum of ceil(dist[i]/s) for all but the last ride, plus dist[last]/s. It never increases with s, so binary search s in [1, 10<sup>7</sup>].

title: Min Days to Make M Bouquets
statement: Flowers grow in a single row; flower i opens on day bloomDay[i] and stays open. A bunch needs k neighbouring open flowers, and each flower can be used in only one bunch. Return the earliest day on which you can pick m bunches, or -1 if it is never possible.
hint: If m·k > n the answer is −1. Otherwise binary search the day; for a given day scan the row counting runs of open flowers.

title: Magnetic Force Between Two Balls
statement: Along a straight coast there are possible beacon spots at distinct positions position (in any order). You must place m beacons on m different spots so that the smallest distance between any two beacons is as large as possible. Return that largest possible minimum distance.
hint: Sort the spots. For a candidate gap g, greedily place beacons left to right whenever the distance from the last one is ≥ g; binary search the largest g that fits m beacons.

title: Split Array Largest Sum
statement: A book has chapters with page counts nums in reading order. Split the chapters into exactly k non-empty groups of consecutive chapters (one group per reader). Return the smallest possible value of the largest group's total page count.
constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10<sup>6</sup>, sum(nums) ≤ 10<sup>9</sup>, 1 ≤ k ≤ min(50, nums.length)
hint: Binary search the answer between max(nums) and sum(nums). For a limit, greedily count how many groups are needed; if it is ≤ k the limit is achievable.

title: Valid Parentheses
statement: The string s contains only the characters ()[]{}. Return true if every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket, in the correct nesting order, and every closing bracket has a matching opener.
hint: Push openers on a stack. On a closer, the top of the stack must be its matching opener; at the end the stack must be empty.

title: Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid
statement: Given a string s of ( and ), you may insert parentheses anywhere. Return the minimum number of insertions needed so that the string becomes balanced (every ( has a later matching ) and vice versa).
hint: Track the number of currently open '('. A ')' with nothing open needs an inserted '('; whatever stays open at the end needs that many ')'.

title: Score of Parentheses
statement:
A balanced string s of parentheses is scored like this:

  • () is worth 1 point.
  • Two balanced strings side by side, AB, are worth score(A) + score(B).
  • A balanced string wrapped in a pair, (A), is worth 2 · score(A).

Return the score of s.
hint: Use a stack of partial scores: on '(' push 0; on ')' pop v and add max(2·v, 1) to the new top.

title: Longest Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string s made of ( and ), return the length of its longest contiguous substring that is a balanced parentheses string. Return 0 if there is none.
hint: Keep a stack of indices, seeded with −1 as a base. Push '(' indices; on ')' pop, and if the stack becomes empty push the current index as the new base, else the length is i − top.

title: Backspace String Compare
statement: Two people type on old keyboards where # is an erase key that deletes the previous character (erasing on an empty line does nothing). Given what they typed, s and t, return true if both screens end up showing the same text.
hint: Simulate each screen with a stack: push letters, pop on '#'. (Bonus: scan both strings backwards with skip counters for O(1) extra space.)

title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates
statement: In a word game, whenever two identical letters stand next to each other, both disappear and the gap closes. This repeats until no two neighbours are equal. Given the starting string s, return the final string (it is unique).
hint: Scan left to right with a stack: if the current letter equals the top, pop; otherwise push.

title: Make the String Great
statement: Two neighbouring characters cancel each other when they are the same letter in different cases (like q and Q, in either order). Keep removing cancelling pairs from s until none remain and return what is left (possibly the empty string).
hint: Push characters on a stack; if the new one and the top are the same letter with different case, pop instead.

title: Minimum String Length After Removing Substrings
statement: The string s contains uppercase letters. In one move you may delete any occurrence of the substring "AB" or "CD"; the remaining parts join together and may form new occurrences. Return the smallest length the string can reach.
hint: Scan with a stack: when the top and current character form AB or CD, pop instead of pushing. The stack size at the end is the answer.

title: Implement Queue using Stacks
statement:
Build a first-in-first-out queue using only stack operations (push to top, pop from top, peek top, size, is empty). Implement push(x) (add to the back), pop() (remove and return the front), peek() (return the front) and empty().

Input line 1 is the list of operations (the first one builds the object), line 2 their arguments. The output lists each call's return value (null for calls that return nothing).
constraints: Up to 10<sup>5</sup> calls per test; pop/peek are only called on a non-empty queue.
hint: Use an 'in' stack for pushes and an 'out' stack for pops. Only when 'out' is empty, move everything from 'in' to 'out' — this reverses the order. Amortised O(1).

title: Implement Stack using Queues
statement:
Build a last-in-first-out stack using only queue operations (add to back, remove from front, look at front, size, is empty). Implement push(x), pop() (remove and return the top), top() and empty().

Input line 1 is the list of operations (the first one builds the object), line 2 their arguments. The output lists each call's return value (null for calls that return nothing).
constraints: Tests have up to 3000 calls; pop/top are only called on a non-empty stack.
hint: After adding x to the back of a single queue, rotate the queue (remove from front and re-add) size−1 times so x ends up at the front.

title: Min Stack
statement:
Design a stack of numbered plates that supports push(val), pop(), top() (return the top value) and getMin() (return the smallest value currently in the stack). Every operation must run in O(1) time.

Input line 1 is the list of operations (the first one builds the object), line 2 their arguments. The output lists each call's return value (null for calls that return nothing).
constraints: Up to 1.2·10<sup>5</sup> calls per test; pop/top/getMin only on a non-empty stack. −1000 ≤ val ≤ 1000.
hint: Store each value together with the minimum of the stack at the moment it was pushed.

title: Design Stack with Increment Operation
statement:
Design CustomStack(maxSize), a stack that holds at most maxSize numbers.

  • push(x): put x on top, unless the stack is already full (then do nothing).
  • pop(): remove and return the top, or return -1 if the stack is empty.
  • increment(k, val): add val to each of the bottom k elements (or to all of them if there are fewer than k).

Input line 1 is the list of operations (the first one builds the object), line 2 their arguments. The output lists each call's return value (null for calls that return nothing).
constraints: 1 ≤ maxSize ≤ 3·10<sup>4</sup>, 1 ≤ x ≤ 1000, 1 ≤ k ≤ 3·10<sup>4</sup>, 0 ≤ val ≤ 100, up to 10<sup>5</sup> calls per test
hint: Lazy increments: store inc[i] for the index min(k, size)−1. When popping index i, add inc[i] to the returned value and pass inc[i] down to inc[i−1].

title: Next Greater Element I
statement: line lists distinct numbers, and queries is a list of some of those numbers (each distinct). For each query value, find where it sits in line and return the first value to its right that is larger, or -1 if none exists. Return the answers in query order.
constraints: 1 ≤ queries.length ≤ line.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, all values distinct within each array
hint: Walk through line with a decreasing stack; when a bigger value arrives it is the answer for everything it pops. Store answers in a map keyed by value.

title: Next Greater Element II
statement: Guests sit around a round table, and nums[i] is the number on guest i's card. Going clockwise (increasing index, wrapping from the last guest back to the first), find for each guest the first card strictly larger than theirs. Return these values, using -1 where no larger card exists.
hint: Loop over indices 0..2n−1 using i mod n, keeping a stack of indices with decreasing values still waiting for an answer.

title: Daily Temperatures
statement: temps[i] is the forecast temperature for day i. For every day, return how many days you have to wait until a strictly warmer day arrives. If no warmer day comes, the answer for that day is 0.
hint: Keep a stack of day indices with non-increasing temperatures. A warmer day pops every colder day and fills in their waits.

title: Online Stock Span
statement:
Design StockSpanner, which receives one daily price at a time through next(price). Each call returns the price's streak: the number of consecutive days, ending today and going backwards, whose price was less than or equal to today's price (today counts).

Input line 1 is the list of operations (the first one builds the object), line 2 their arguments. The output lists each call's return value (null for calls that return nothing).
hint: Keep a stack of (price, streak) pairs with decreasing prices. When a new price arrives, pop every pair with price ≤ it and add their streaks to its own.

title: Asteroid Collision
statement: Carts sit on a track in the order given by carts. The absolute value is a cart's weight; the sign is its direction (positive = right, negative = left). All carts move at the same speed. When two meet, the lighter one is destroyed; if they weigh the same, both are destroyed. Carts moving the same way never meet. Return the carts that remain, in order.
hint: Use a stack of survivors. A left-moving cart fights the right-moving carts on top of the stack until it is destroyed or no right-mover remains.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
statement: A row of buildings, each 1 unit wide, has heights heights. You want to hang one rectangular banner flat against the buildings: it must cover a contiguous range of buildings and cannot be taller than the shortest building in that range. Return the largest possible banner area.
hint: Keep a stack of indices with increasing heights. When a shorter bar arrives, pop bars; each popped bar's widest rectangle spans from the new stack top + 1 to the current index − 1.

title: Maximal Rectangle
statement: A roof is described by a grid roof of characters: '1' means the cell can hold a solar panel and '0' means it cannot. Return the area of the largest axis-aligned rectangle made only of '1' cells.
hint: Process the grid row by row, keeping for each column how many consecutive '1's end at this row. Each row then becomes a histogram — find its largest rectangle with a monotonic stack.

title: Basic Calculator II
statement: The string s is a valid arithmetic expression made of non-negative integers, the operators + - * / and spaces (no parentheses). Evaluate it with the usual precedence (* and / before + and -, left to right otherwise) and return the result. Division truncates toward zero. Do not use an eval function.
constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 3·10<sup>5</sup>; all intermediate results fit in a 32-bit signed integer; no division by zero
hint: Keep a stack of terms. Push +num or −num for + and −; for * and / combine immediately with the top of the stack. The answer is the sum of the stack.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
statement:
An expression is written in postfix form: each operator comes after its two operands. tokens lists the tokens; each is an integer or one of + - * /. Evaluate the expression and return its value. Division truncates toward zero.

For example ["5","1","-","3","*"] means (5 − 1) · 3 = 12.
constraints: 1 ≤ tokens.length ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>; the expression is valid; no division by zero; all values fit in 32 bits
hint: Push numbers on a stack. For an operator pop b then a, push a op b. Careful: truncate division toward zero, not floor.

title: Decode String
statement:
A compressed message uses the rule k[text], meaning text written k times. Codes can be nested and mixed with plain lowercase letters. Given a valid compressed string s, return the fully expanded message.

For example 2[ab3[c]] expands to abcccabccc.
constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 100, 1 ≤ k ≤ 300, digits only appear as repeat counts, expanded length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>
hint: Use a stack of (text built so far, repeat count). On '[' push and start fresh; on ']' pop and set current = saved + count · current.

title: Basic Calculator I
statement: Evaluate the valid expression s, which contains non-negative integers, +, -, parentheses and spaces. A - may also be used as a negation sign (for example -(2+3) or -4), but + is never unary. Return the result without using an eval function.
constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 3·10<sup>5</sup>; all results fit in a 32-bit signed integer
hint: Scan left to right keeping a running result and a sign. On '(' push (result, sign) and reset; on ')' finish the inner value, multiply by the saved sign and add the saved result.

title: Remove K Digits
statement: num is a string of digits representing a non-negative integer (no leading zeros unless it is "0"). Delete exactly k digits so the remaining number is as small as possible. Return it as a string without leading zeros; return "0" if nothing (or only zeros) remains.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ num.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup> (k may also be 0 in tests)
hint: Keep an increasing stack of digits: while the top is bigger than the current digit and you still have deletions left, pop. Remove leftover deletions from the end.

title: Remove Duplicate Letters
statement: Delete letters from s so that every distinct letter of s appears exactly once, keeping the remaining letters in their original order. Among all possible results, return the alphabetically smallest one.
hint: Record each letter's last index. Build a stack; skip letters already in it; while the top is bigger than the current letter and appears again later, pop it.

title: Smallest Subsequence of Distinct Characters
statement: A label maker can print any subsequence of the string text. Print a subsequence that contains every distinct letter of text exactly once. If there are several, return the one that comes first in dictionary order.
hint: Greedy monotonic stack: a larger letter on top can be dropped if it occurs again later in text; never add a letter that is already in the stack.

title: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses
statement: The string s contains lowercase letters and parentheses. Pair up parentheses the usual way: scanning left to right, each ) pairs with the nearest earlier ( that is still unpaired. Delete every parenthesis that ends up without a partner (and nothing else) and return the resulting string. The result is balanced and uses the fewest deletions.
hint: Push indices of '(' on a stack; a ')' with an empty stack is marked for deletion, otherwise pop. Indices left on the stack at the end are deleted too.

title: Create Maximum Number
statement: Two rows of digit tiles are given as a and b (each value 0–9). Pick exactly k tiles in total from the two rows, keeping the relative order of tiles taken from the same row, and arrange them into one sequence to form the largest possible number. Return that sequence of k digits.
hint: For each split i + (k−i), take the best i digits from a and k−i from b with a monotonic stack, then merge the two greedily by comparing the remaining suffixes. Keep the largest result.

title: Fibonacci Number
statement:
A sequence starts with 0 and 1, and every later term is the sum of the two terms right before it. Given n, return term number n (0-indexed).

For instance term 6 is 8, because the sequence goes 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.
hint: f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2) with base cases f(0)=0, f(1)=1. Memoize or iterate to avoid exponential work.

title: Climbing Stairs
statement:
A tower has n steps. With each move you go up either 1 step or 2 steps. Return how many different move sequences take you from the ground exactly to the top step.

With 3 steps there are 3 ways: 1+1+1, 1+2 and 2+1.
hint: The last move was a 1-hop or a 2-hop, so ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2).

title: Pow(x, n)
statement:
Compute x raised to the integer power n and return it as a decimal number. n may be negative (meaning 1 divided by x|n|) and can be huge, so multiplying x by itself n times is too slow. Do not use a built-in power function.

Answers are accepted within 10−5.
hint: x<sup>n</sup> = (x<sup>n/2</sup>)<sup>2</sup>, times one extra x when n is odd. That halves n on every recursive call.

title: Unique Paths
statement: A robot stands in the top-left cell of a grid with rows rows and cols columns. Each move takes it one cell right or one cell down. Return how many different routes bring it to the bottom-right cell.
hint: routes(r, c) = routes(r−1, c) + routes(r, c−1), with 1 route along the first row and column. Memoize or fill a table.

title: House Robber
statement: Coins lie in a line; coins[i] is the value of pile i. You may take any piles you like, except that you may never take two piles that sit next to each other. Return the largest total value you can collect.
hint: best(i) = max(best(i−1), best(i−2) + coins[i]): either skip pile i or take it and skip its left neighbour.

title: Reverse a Linked List
statement: Reverse the singly linked list starting at head and return its new head. Try to do it with recursion: reverse everything after the first node, then attach the first node at the end.
hint: rev(head): if head or head.next is null return head; newHead = rev(head.next); head.next.next = head; head.next = null.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
statement: You get the heads of two linked lists a and b, each sorted in non-decreasing order. Combine all of their nodes into one sorted list and return its head.
hint: The smaller head goes first; its next is the merge of the rest. Recurse, or use a dummy node and a tail pointer.

title: Subsets
statement:
Given an array items of distinct integers, return every possible selection of them (including the empty selection and the full one). Each selection appears once.

You may return the selections in any order, and the numbers inside each selection in any order.
hint: For each element decide include / exclude and recurse on the rest; 2<sup>n</sup> leaves = 2<sup>n</sup> selections.

title: Target Sum
statement:
Put a + or a − sign in front of every number in nums (keeping their order) and add everything up. Return how many of the sign choices make the total equal goal.

Two choices are different if at least one position has a different sign, even when the numbers are equal.
hint: count(i, sum) = count(i+1, sum+nums[i]) + count(i+1, sum−nums[i]); memoize on (i, sum).

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
statement:
Arrays a and b are each sorted in non-decreasing order. Imagine merging them into one sorted array; return its median (the middle value, or the average of the two middle values when the combined length is even).

Aim for O(log(m+n)) time by discarding half of the remaining candidates at each step instead of merging.
hint: Find the k-th smallest recursively: compare a[k/2−1] and b[k/2−1]; the side with the smaller value can drop its first k/2 elements.

title: Middle of the Linked List
statement: Return the list that starts at the middle node of the linked list head. When there are two middle nodes (even length), use the second one.
hint: Move a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps; when fast runs out, slow is in the middle.

title: Linked List Cycle
statement:
A trail of n markers is described by the array next: from marker i you walk to marker next[i], and -1 means the trail ends there. You start at marker 0 (when n > 0). Return true if walking forever is possible because you eventually revisit a marker, otherwise false.

Try to use O(1) extra memory.
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>; every marker is reachable from marker 0; each marker is pointed to by at most one marker, except possibly the marker where a loop closes
hint: Floyd's tortoise and hare: a slow index moves one step, a fast index two. They meet only if there is a loop.

title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
statement:
Markers are numbered 0..n−1 and next[i] is the marker after i (-1 = end). Two trails start at startA and startB; neither trail loops. Once two trails reach a common marker they share every marker after it. Return the first marker both trails visit, or -1 if they never meet.

Try for O(1) extra memory.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>; every marker lies on at least one of the two trails
hint: Walk pointer p from A and q from B; when one falls off the end, restart it at the other trail's start. After at most lenA+lenB steps they meet at the junction (or both at -1).

title: Remove Nth Node from End
statement:
Remove the k-th node counting from the end of the linked list head (k = 1 is the last node) and return the head of the resulting list.

Can you do it in one pass?
hint: Use a dummy node. Move a lead pointer k steps ahead, then move both until the lead hits the last node; the trailing pointer sits just before the one to delete.

title: Linked List Cycle II
statement:
As before, next[i] is the marker you walk to from marker i (-1 = end), and the walk starts at marker 0. If the walk enters a loop, return the first marker of the loop (the marker where the loop is entered); otherwise return -1.

Try to use O(1) extra memory.
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>; every marker is reachable from marker 0
hint: After slow and fast meet inside the loop, restart one pointer at marker 0 and step both by one; they meet again exactly at the entrance.

title: Odd-Even Linked List
statement:
Rearrange the linked list head so that all nodes in odd positions (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) come first, followed by all nodes in even positions (2nd, 4th, …). Keep the original relative order inside each group and return the new head.

Positions are about where a node sits, not its value. Use O(1) extra space.
hint: Keep two tails, odd and even, and splice nodes alternately onto them; finally attach the even chain after the odd chain.

title: Design Linked List
statement:
Implement a list class ChainList (indexes are 0-based) on top of your own nodes:

  • get(index): value at index, or -1 if the index is invalid.
  • addAtHead(val) / addAtTail(val): insert at the front / back.
  • addAtIndex(index, val): insert so the new value ends up at index; if index equals the length append it, if it is larger do nothing.
  • deleteAtIndex(index): remove the element at index if it exists.

Line 1 lists the operations, line 2 their arguments; output each call's return (null for void calls).
hint: A dummy (sentinel) head node removes the special case for index 0; walk index steps to find the node before the target.

title: Palindrome Linked List
statement:
Return true if the values of the linked list head read the same from front to back as from back to front, otherwise false.

Follow-up: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
hint: Find the middle with fast/slow pointers, reverse the second half, then compare the two halves node by node.

title: Reverse Linked List II
statement: Positions in the linked list head are counted from 1. Reverse only the nodes from position lo through position hi (inclusive), leave the rest untouched, and return the head.
hint: Walk to the node just before position lo (a dummy head helps when lo = 1), then repeatedly move the next node to the front of the stretch, hi−lo times.

title: Maximum Twin Sum of a Linked List
statement: The linked list head has an even number of nodes n. The node at 0-based position i is partnered with the node at position n−1−i (first with last, second with second-to-last, …). Return the largest sum of a node's value and its partner's value.
hint: Reverse the second half in place, then walk the first half and the reversed half together, summing pairs.

title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
statement: In the linked list head, swap the 1st node with the 2nd, the 3rd with the 4th, and so on; a final unpaired node stays where it is. Swap the nodes themselves by relinking them (don't just exchange values) and return the new head.
hint: Recursively: second = head.next; head.next = swap(second.next); second.next = head; return second.

title: Rotate List
statement: Rotate the linked list head to the right by k places: each rotation moves the last node to the front. Return the new head. Note that k can be much larger than the list length.
hint: Find the length L and tail; only k mod L rotations matter. Link the tail to the head to form a ring, then cut it L − (k mod L) nodes from the start.

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
statement:
Split the linked list head into consecutive blocks of k nodes, starting from the front, and reverse the nodes inside every complete block. A final block with fewer than k nodes keeps its original order. Relink nodes (don't just change values) and return the new head.

Aim for O(1) extra memory.
hint: Check that k nodes remain ahead; reverse exactly those k with the usual prev/cur loop, connect the previous block's tail to the new block head, and move on.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
statement: The linked list head is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove extra copies so that every value appears exactly once, and return the head of the (still sorted) list.
hint: Walk the list; while the next node has the same value as the current one, skip it by relinking current.next.

title: Add Two Numbers
statement:
Two non-negative integers are stored as linked lists a and b, one decimal digit per node, with the ones digit first. Neither has leading zeros except the number 0 itself. Return their sum in the same backwards-digit format.

For example 342 is stored as 2 → 4 → 3.
hint: Walk both lists together, adding digits plus a carry; create a node for sum % 10 and carry sum // 10. Don't forget a final carry.

title: Sort List
statement: Sort the linked list head in ascending order and return the new head. Aim for O(n log n) time by working directly on the nodes rather than copying values into an array.
hint: Merge sort: split at the middle with slow/fast pointers, sort both halves recursively, then merge two sorted lists.

title: Reorder List
statement: Given the linked list L0 → L1 → … → Ln−1, relink its nodes into the order L0 → Ln−1 → L1 → Ln−2 → L2 → … (alternately taking from the front and the back). Return the head (which is still L0). Rearrange the nodes themselves, not just their values.
hint: Three steps: find the middle, reverse the second half, then interleave the two halves.

title: Partition List
statement: Rearrange the linked list head so that every node with a value smaller than pivot comes before every node with a value greater than or equal to pivot. Inside each of the two groups keep the original relative order. Return the new head.
hint: Build two chains with dummy heads (small and big), append each node to the right one, then join small's tail to big's head and end big with null.

title: Copy List with Random Pointer
statement:
A linked list is stored in scrambled memory slots 0..n−1: slot i holds value vals[i], its successor slot next[i] (-1 = end) and a shortcut slot shortcut[i] pointing to any node of the list (-1 = none). The list starts at slot head (-1 = empty).

Make a deep copy laid out in list order and return it as one pair per node, from first to last: [value, p], where p is the 0-based list position of the node its shortcut points to, or -1.
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 2.5·10<sup>4</sup>, −100 ≤ vals[i] ≤ 100; every slot is on the list
hint: Map each old slot to its new node (or new position) in a first pass along next, then fill in the shortcuts with that map in a second pass.

title: Merge K Sorted Lists
statement: You receive an array lists of linked lists, each sorted in non-decreasing order (some may be empty). Merge all of them into a single sorted linked list and return its head.
hint: Keep a min-heap of the current head of each list (or merge lists pairwise, divide-and-conquer style) for O(N log k).

title: LRU Cache
statement:
Design RecentCache(capacity), a key→value store holding at most capacity keys:

  • get(key): the key's value, or -1 if absent. A successful get counts as a use.
  • put(key, value): insert or overwrite the key (this is a use). If a new key makes the store exceed capacity, first evict the key whose last use is the oldest.

Both operations should run in O(1) on average. Line 1 lists the operations, line 2 their arguments; output each call's return (null for void calls).
constraints: 1 ≤ capacity ≤ 3000, 0 ≤ key ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>, 0 ≤ value ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>, at most 5·10<sup>4</sup> calls
hint: A hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency: move a node to the front on each use and evict from the back.

title: Flatten Multilevel DLL
statement:
Nodes 0..n−1 form a layered list: node i has value vals[i], a successor next[i] on its own layer and possibly a child[i] that starts a lower layer (-1 = none). The top layer starts at node 0.

Flatten it: whenever a node has a child layer, that entire (already flattened) child layer comes right after the node and before the node's own successor. Return the values in flattened order.
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 1000, values are distinct, every node belongs to exactly one layer and the layers form a tree (no cycles)
hint: DFS: visit a node, then recursively flatten its child layer, then continue with next. An explicit stack (push next, then child) avoids deep recursion.

title: LFU Cache
statement:
Design FreqCache(capacity), a key→value store holding at most capacity keys. Every key has a use counter: inserting a new key sets it to 1, and each successful get or overwriting put adds 1.

  • get(key): the value, or -1 if absent.
  • put(key, value): insert or overwrite. If inserting a new key would exceed capacity, first evict the key with the smallest use counter; among ties, evict the one whose last use is the oldest.

Target O(1) per operation. Line 1 lists the operations, line 2 their arguments; output each call's return (null for void calls).
constraints: 1 ≤ capacity ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>, 0 ≤ key ≤ 2·10<sup>4</sup>, 0 ≤ value ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>, at most 5·10<sup>4</sup> calls
hint: Map key → (value, count) and count → an ordered list (doubly linked) of keys by recency; track the current minimum count, which resets to 1 on every insertion.

title: Inorder Traversal
statement:
Walk the binary tree so that for every node you first visit its whole left subtree, then the node itself, then its whole right subtree. Return the node values in the order you visited them.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Recurse left, record the value, recurse right — or simulate it with an explicit stack that keeps sliding left.

title: Symmetric Tree
statement:
A tree is a mirror image of itself if folding it down the vertical line through the root makes every node land on a node with the same value. Return true if the tree has this property, otherwise false. An empty tree counts as symmetric.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Compare two subtrees at once: a.left must mirror b.right and a.right must mirror b.left, with equal values at a and b.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
statement:
Return the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes of the tree. The path does not have to pass through the root. An empty tree or a single node gives 0.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: For each node, the longest path bending there is height(left) + height(right). Compute heights bottom-up and keep the best sum.

title: Balanced Binary Tree
statement:
Call a tree evenly weighted if, at every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Return true if the given tree is evenly weighted. An empty tree is.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Return the height from a post-order DFS, or −1 as soon as any node is out of balance so the failure bubbles up in O(n).

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
statement:
Return the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to any leaf. An empty tree has height 0.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)), with height(null) = 0.

title: Path Sum
statement:
Each node holds an integer. Return true if some path that starts at the root and ends at a leaf (a node with no children) has values summing to exactly target. An empty tree has no such path.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Subtract each node's value from the target as you go down; at a leaf check whether what remains equals that leaf's value.

title: Subtree of Another Tree
statement:
You get a big tree root and a small non-empty tree sub. Return true if some node of root, together with all of its descendants, forms a tree identical to sub (same shape and same values), otherwise false.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
constraints: 1 ≤ nodes in root ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, 1 ≤ nodes in sub ≤ 2000, depth ≤ 3000
hint: For each node of root, run a 'same tree' check against sub. O(n·m) is fine here; tree hashing or serialization makes it linear.

title: Path Sum II
statement:
List every root-to-leaf path whose values add up to target. Each path is the list of values from the root down to the leaf. Return the paths ordered by their leaf from left to right (the order a left-first DFS reaches them). Return an empty list if there are none.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: DFS with one shared path list: push the node, recurse left then right, pop on the way back. Copy the path when a leaf matches.

title: Path Sum III
statement:
A downward run is a path that starts at any node and moves only from parents to children, ending at any node below it (or at the start node itself). Count the downward runs whose values sum to exactly target.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Keep a hashmap of prefix sums along the current root-to-node path. At each node, add count[prefix − target], recurse, then undo the node's prefix.

title: Count Complete Tree Nodes
statement:
The tree is packed: every level is completely full except possibly the last, and the last level's nodes are pushed as far left as possible. Return how many nodes it has. Try to do better than visiting every node.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Compare the leftmost depth and rightmost depth of a subtree: if equal it is perfect and has 2^h − 1 nodes; otherwise recurse into both children. That is O(log² n).

title: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree
statement:
All node values in the tree are distinct. Starting from the node whose value is target, you may move along any edge (to a child or to the parent). Return the values of all nodes exactly k edges away, sorted in ascending order.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
constraints: 1 ≤ nodes ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, depth ≤ 3000, values distinct, target exists, 0 ≤ k ≤ 3000
hint: Record each node's parent with a DFS, then BFS from the target treating the tree as an undirected graph for k rounds.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
statement:
A path is any sequence of nodes connected by edges where no node repeats; it may start and end anywhere and need not touch the root, but must contain at least one node. Return the largest possible sum of values along a path.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: For each node compute the best downward 'arm' (val + max(0, best child arm)). The best path bending at the node is val + max(0, leftArm) + max(0, rightArm).

title: Binary Tree Cameras
statement:
You may build a watchtower on any node. A tower watches its own node, its parent and its children. Return the minimum number of towers needed so that every node in the tree is watched. (Node values don't matter.)

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Greedy post-order with three states: 'needs cover', 'covered without tower', 'has tower'. Put a tower on a parent whenever any child needs cover; leaves never get towers.

title: Average of Levels in Binary Tree
statement:
Treat each depth of the tree as a floor. Return a list with the average of the node values on each floor, from the root's floor downwards. Answers within 10−5 are accepted.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: BFS one level at a time: sum the values in the current queue and divide by its size.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
statement:
Return the tree's values grouped by depth: one inner list per depth, starting from the root, each listing that depth's values from left to right.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Use a queue; before processing a level remember its size so you know where the level ends.

title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
statement:
Group the tree's values by depth like a row-by-row read, but alternate direction: the root's row is read left to right, the next row right to left, the next left to right again, and so on. Return the list of rows.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Do a normal level-order BFS and reverse every second row (or append to the front of a deque on odd levels).

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
statement:
Imagine standing to the right of the tree and looking at it. On each depth you see only the rightmost node. Return the values you see, from the top depth to the bottom.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Level-order BFS and take the last node of every level — or DFS visiting right before left and record the first node seen at each new depth.

title: Vertical Order Traversal
statement:
Place the root at row 0, column 0. A node at (row r, column c) has its left child at (r+1, c−1) and right child at (r+1, c+1). Return the values column by column from the leftmost column to the rightmost. Inside a column list the values from top row to bottom row; if several nodes share the same row and column, list them by smaller value first.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Collect (column, row, value) triples with BFS or DFS, sort them, then split into groups by column.

title: Maximum Width of Binary Tree
statement:
The width of a level is the number of positions between its leftmost and rightmost nodes, inclusive, counting the empty spots that would be filled if the tree were complete down to that level. Return the largest width over all levels. The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Number positions like a heap (children 2i and 2i+1). Width of a level = last − first + 1. Re-base positions per level (subtract the level's first index) to keep numbers small.

title: Invert Binary Tree
statement:
Swap the left and right child of every node in the tree, producing its mirror image, and return the root of the result.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Recursively flip both subtrees, then swap them (or use a queue and swap children of each node you visit).

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of Binary Tree
statement:
All values in the tree are distinct, and p and q are values of two different nodes in it. Return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree. A node counts as being in its own subtree.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
constraints: 2 ≤ nodes ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, depth ≤ 3000, values distinct, p ≠ q, both present
hint: Recurse: if the current node is p or q return it; otherwise search both sides. If both sides return something, the current node is the answer.

title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
statement:
Rearrange the tree in place into a single chain: every node's left becomes null and its right points to the next node in pre-order (node, then left subtree, then right subtree). Your function returns nothing; we read the tree from root afterwards.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: For each node with a left subtree, find the rightmost node of that left subtree, hang the old right subtree there, move left to right, and continue down the chain (O(1) extra space).

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder & Inorder
statement:
A tree with distinct values was walked twice: preorder lists node, left subtree, right subtree; inorder lists left subtree, node, right subtree. Rebuild the tree and return its root.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: The first preorder value is the root; its position in inorder splits the left and right subtrees. Use a value→index map so each split is O(1).

title: Construct Binary Tree from Inorder & Postorder
statement:
A tree with distinct values was walked twice: inorder lists left subtree, node, right subtree; postorder lists left subtree, right subtree, then node. Rebuild the tree and return its root.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: The last postorder value is the root. Consume postorder from the back, building the right subtree before the left, and split inorder with a value→index map.

title: Kth Ancestor of a Tree Node
statement:
A rooted tree has nodes 0..n−1; parent[i] is the parent of node i and parent[0] = −1 (node 0 is the root). Build AncestorFinder(n, parent) and answer many calls kthAncestor(node, k): return the node reached by moving up k parents from node, or −1 if you would go past the root.

Input line 1 is the list of operations, line 2 their arguments. The output lists each call's return value (null for the constructor).
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 5·10<sup>4</sup>, 1 ≤ k ≤ n, up to 1.8·10<sup>4</sup> queries
hint: Binary lifting: up[j][v] = the 2^j-th ancestor of v. Answer a query by jumping along the set bits of k.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
statement:
Build a class TreeCodec that converts trees to text and back using this exact format: list the nodes in pre-order (node, left subtree, right subtree), write each value as a decimal number and every missing child as #, and join everything with commas. For example a root 1 with only a left child 2 becomes 1,2,#,#,#, and an empty tree becomes #.

encode(root) returns the text; decode(data) returns the rebuilt tree. Input line 1 is the list of operations, line 2 their arguments; the output lists each call's return value (null for the constructor).

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Encode with a pre-order DFS that emits # for null. Decode by reading tokens with a shared index: a number makes a node and recursively reads its left then right; # returns null.

title: Convert Sorted Array to BST
statement:
nums is strictly increasing. Build a height-balanced binary search tree from it with this rule: the root is the middle element (for an even count, the left of the two middle elements, i.e. index (lo + hi) / 2 rounded down), and the left and right halves are built the same way. Return the root.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Recurse on index ranges [lo, hi]: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 becomes the node, [lo, mid−1] its left subtree, [mid+1, hi] its right subtree.

title: Search in a BST
statement:
The tree is a binary search tree with distinct keys (left subtree smaller, right subtree larger). Find the node whose value equals key and return it — the whole subtree hanging from it. Return an empty tree (null) if the key is absent.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Walk from the root: go left if key is smaller, right if larger, stop when equal. O(height).

title: Insert into a BST
statement:
Insert key (guaranteed not already present) into the binary search tree by walking down from the root — left when the key is smaller than the current node, right when larger — and attaching it as a new leaf at the first empty spot. Return the root (which is the new node if the tree was empty).

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Same walk as a search; when the child you need to move into is null, put the new node there.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
statement:
Return true if the tree is a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly smaller and all values in its right subtree are strictly larger. Duplicates are not allowed. An empty tree is valid.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Checking only direct children is not enough. Pass down an open interval (low, high) that each node must lie in, or check that the in-order walk is strictly increasing.

title: Delete Node in a BST
statement:
Remove the node with value key from the binary search tree (distinct keys) and return the root. Use exactly this rule so the result is unique:

  • Key absent: return the tree unchanged.
  • Node has no left child: replace it with its right subtree. Otherwise, if it has no right child: replace it with its left subtree.
  • Two children: copy the value of its in-order successor (smallest value in its right subtree) into the node, then remove that successor from the right subtree by the same rule.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Recurse to find the key, returning the possibly-new subtree root at each step: root.left = delete(root.left, key) and so on.

title: Kth Smallest Element in BST
statement:
Given a binary search tree with distinct keys and a number k (1-based), return the k-th smallest key in the tree.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: An in-order walk of a BST visits keys in ascending order; stop after the k-th visit.

title: Convert BST to Greater Tree
statement:
In a binary search tree with distinct keys, replace every node's value with its original value plus the sum of all original values greater than it. Keep the shape unchanged and return the root.
