Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Do a reverse in-order walk (right, node, left) carrying a running total; add it into each node as you pass.

title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
statement:
Design SortedWalker(root) over a binary search tree. next() returns the next key in ascending order (it is only called when one remains), and hasNext() says whether any key remains. Aim for O(height) memory, so don't copy the whole tree into a list.

Input line 1 is the list of operations, line 2 their arguments (the constructor gets the tree in level order). The output lists each call's return value (null for the constructor).
hint: Keep a stack of the left spine. next() pops a node, then pushes the left spine of its right child. Amortized O(1) per call.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of BST
statement:
The tree is a binary search tree with distinct keys, and p and q are two different keys in it. Return the key of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node having both in its subtree (a node is in its own subtree). Use the ordering — no need to search the whole tree.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
constraints: 2 ≤ nodes ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, depth ≤ 3000, keys distinct, p ≠ q, both present
hint: From the root: if both keys are smaller go left, if both are larger go right; otherwise the current node is where their paths split.

title: Recover BST
statement:
Someone took a valid binary search tree with distinct keys and swapped the values of exactly two nodes. Repair it in place by swapping those two values back, without changing the shape. Your function returns nothing; we read the tree from root afterwards.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: In-order the values should rise. The first node that is bigger than its successor, and the last node that is smaller than its predecessor, are the swapped pair.

title: Maximum Sum BST in Binary Tree
statement:
Look at every node's full subtree (the node plus all its descendants). Among the subtrees that are valid binary search trees (left side strictly smaller, right side strictly larger, at every node), return the largest sum of values. The empty subtree counts and has sum 0, so the answer is never negative.

Trees are given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Post-order DFS returning (isBST, min, max, sum) for each subtree; a node is a BST root when both children are and left.max < val < right.min.

title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
statement:
A game shows the score that currently sits in k-th place (k-th largest, counting duplicates). Build class KthTracker: the constructor receives k and the starting scores nums; each call add(val) records a new score and returns the current k-th largest score.

Input line 1 lists the operations, line 2 their arguments; the output lists each call's return (null for the constructor).
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>, 0 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>, at most 3·10<sup>4</sup> calls to add, at least k scores exist after every add, −10<sup>4</sup> ≤ values ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>
hint: Keep a min-heap holding only the k largest scores; its top is the answer. Push, then pop while size exceeds k.

title: Last Stone Weight
statement: A crusher repeatedly takes the two heaviest boulders, weights x ≤ y, and smashes them together. If x == y both vanish; otherwise one boulder of weight y − x goes back into the pile. When at most one boulder is left, return its weight, or 0 if none remain.
hint: Use a max-heap (store negatives with heapq) and pop two at a time.

title: Top K Frequent Words
statement: You get a list of hashtags words (repeats allowed) and an integer k. Return the k most used tags, ordered from most to least frequent. Tags with the same count are ordered alphabetically.
constraints: 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, 1 ≤ words[i].length ≤ 10, 1 ≤ k ≤ number of distinct words, lowercase letters only
hint: Count with a hash map, then take the k best using a heap keyed by (−count, word).

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
statement: Given an unsorted array nums and an integer k, return the value that would be at position k if the array were sorted from largest to smallest (duplicates count separately).
hint: A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest values seen so far; its top is the answer. (Quickselect also works.)

title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
statement: Two price lists a and b are sorted in non-decreasing order. A combo picks one item from each list and costs a[i] + b[j]. Consider all a.length × b.length combos and return the k cheapest combo totals in non-decreasing order.
constraints: 1 ≤ a.length, b.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, −10<sup>9</sup> < a[i]+b[j] < 10<sup>9</sup> (values here ≤ 10<sup>4</sup> in size), 1 ≤ k ≤ min(10<sup>4</sup>, a.length·b.length)
hint: Seed a min-heap with (a[i]+b[0], i, 0); each time you pop (i, j), push (i, j+1). Pop k times.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
statement:
Numbers arrive one at a time. Build class RunningMedian with addNum(num) to record a number and findMedian() to return the median of everything recorded so far: the middle value, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even.

Input line 1 lists the operations, line 2 their arguments; the output lists each call's return (null for calls that return nothing).
constraints: −10<sup>5</sup> ≤ num ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, findMedian is only called after at least one addNum, at most 5·10<sup>4</sup> calls
hint: Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced so sizes differ by at most one.

title: Smallest Range Covering K Lists
statement: You get lists, several lists of integers each sorted in non-decreasing order. Find the interval [lo, hi] with the smallest width hi − lo that contains at least one number from every list. If several intervals have the same width, return the one with the smaller lo. Return it as [lo, hi].
hint: Put the first element of each list in a min-heap and track the current maximum. The window is [heap min, max]; pop the min and advance that list, stopping when a list runs out.

title: Task Scheduler
statement: A machine runs jobs, one per time slot. Each job is a capital letter in tasks; jobs can run in any order. Two runs of the same letter must be separated by at least n slots in between. The machine may sit idle for a slot. Return the minimum number of slots needed to finish every job.
hint: Greedily run the jobs with the most remaining copies: a max-heap of counts plus a cooldown queue simulates it. Or use the formula (maxCount−1)(n+1)+#letters with maxCount, capped below by tasks.length.

title: Reorganize String
statement:
Rearrange the letters of s so that no two adjacent characters are equal. Among all such rearrangements return the alphabetically smallest one. If no rearrangement works, return the empty string "".

For example, "aab" can only become "aba".
hint: It's possible iff the most common letter appears at most ⌈n/2⌉ times. Build left to right: try letters in order and pick the first that differs from the previous one and keeps the rest feasible (no letter more than ⌈m/2⌉ of the m remaining, and the just-used letter at most ⌊m/2⌋).

title: Sliding Window Median
statement: A window of size k slides over nums one step at a time, from the left edge to the right edge. For every window position return its median (the middle value, or the average of the two middle values when k is even), in order.
hint: Two heaps (low max-heap, high min-heap) with lazy deletion, or keep the window in a sorted list and insert/remove with binary search.

title: Subsets II
statement: The array nums may contain repeated values. Return every different sub-collection you can pick from it (including the empty one). Two picks are the same if they contain the same values with the same multiplicities. Return them in any order; values inside a pick in any order.
hint: Sort first. While backtracking, at each depth skip a value equal to the previous one at that same depth.

title: Combination Sum
statement: You have coins with distinct values given in coins, and an unlimited supply of each. Return every different multiset of coins whose values add up to exactly target. Return the combinations in any order; coins inside a combination in any order.
hint: Backtrack with a start index: you may reuse coin i (stay at i) but never go back to earlier coins, so each multiset appears once.

title: Combination Sum II
statement: A jar holds coins with values coins (values may repeat). Each physical coin can be used at most once. Return every different multiset of values that adds up to exactly target; the same multiset must not appear twice. Return them in any order; values inside a combination in any order.
hint: Sort, then backtrack moving to j+1 after using coins[j]; at the same depth skip a value equal to the one just tried.

title: Permutations
statement: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return every ordering (arrangement) of all its elements. The list of orderings may be in any order.
hint: Backtrack: at each position try every unused element, mark it used, recurse, then unmark.

title: Permutations II
statement: The array nums may contain duplicates. Return every distinct ordering of all its elements (no ordering may appear twice). The list may be in any order.
hint: Sort, then when choosing the next element skip nums[i] if it equals nums[i−1] and nums[i−1] is not currently used. Or backtrack over a value→count map.

title: Generate Parentheses
statement: Given n, return every string made of exactly n opening ( and n closing ) brackets that is properly balanced (every prefix has at least as many openers as closers). Any order.
hint: Build character by character: add '(' while you have openers left, add ')' only when closers used < openers used.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
statement: Cut the string s into consecutive pieces so that every piece reads the same forwards and backwards. Return every possible way to cut it, each as the list of pieces from left to right. The list of ways may be in any order.
hint: Backtrack on the start index: try every end where s[start..end] is a palindrome, recurse from end+1.

title: Restore IP Addresses
statement: Someone typed an IPv4 address but lost the dots, leaving the digit string s. A valid address is four numbers from 0 to 255 joined by dots, with no number having a leading zero (so 0 is fine but 01 is not). Insert exactly three dots into s (keeping every digit, in order) and return every valid address you can form, in any order.
hint: Backtrack over 4 parts, each 1–3 digits long; reject parts over 255 or with a leading zero, and prune when the remaining length can't fit.

title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
statement: You have weights nums and k buckets. Can every weight be placed in exactly one bucket so that all k buckets end up with the same total weight (and none is empty)? Return true or false.
hint: The bucket target is sum/k. Sort descending and fill buckets one at a time by backtracking; memoize on the bitmask of used weights.

title: Word Search
statement: Given a grid of letters board and a string word, decide whether word can be traced by starting on some cell and repeatedly stepping up, down, left or right, without visiting any cell twice. Return true or false.
constraints: 1 ≤ rows, cols ≤ 6, 1 ≤ word.length ≤ 15, letters only (case matters)
hint: DFS from each cell that matches word[0]; mark the cell as visited while exploring and unmark it on the way back.

title: Path with Maximum Gold
statement: A cave map grid holds the amount of treasure in each chamber; 0 means the chamber is blocked. You may start in any chamber with treasure, collect it, and keep moving up, down, left or right into chambers with treasure, never entering a chamber twice and never entering a 0. You can stop whenever you like. Return the most treasure you can collect.
constraints: 1 ≤ rows, cols ≤ 15, 0 ≤ grid[i][j] ≤ 100, at most 25 non-zero cells
hint: Try every non-zero start and DFS, temporarily zeroing the current cell so it isn't revisited, restoring it afterwards.

title: N-Queens
statement: Place n chess queens on an n × n board so that no two share a row, a column or a diagonal. Return every such board. Each board is a list of n strings, one per row, using Q for a queen and . for an empty square. The list of boards may be in any order.
hint: Place one queen per row; track used columns and both diagonal directions (r−c and r+c) in sets so each check is O(1).

title: Sudoku Solver
statement: Complete the 9×9 number puzzle board in place. Empty cells hold '.'; filled cells hold '1'–'9'. When finished, every row, every column and each of the nine 3×3 blocks must contain each digit 1–9 exactly once. Every puzzle given has exactly one solution. Your function returns nothing; we check board afterwards.
constraints: board is 9×9, the puzzle has a unique solution
hint: Keep, for each row, column and block, which digits are used. Backtrack over empty cells, ideally picking the cell with the fewest options first.

title: Word Search II
statement: Given a letter grid board and a list of distinct candidate words words, return every candidate that can be traced on the grid by moving up, down, left or right between neighbouring cells, using no cell twice within one word. Return the found words in any order.
constraints: 1 ≤ rows, cols ≤ 12, 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 3·10<sup>4</sup>, 1 ≤ words[i].length ≤ 10, lowercase letters
hint: Put all words in a trie and DFS from every cell, walking the trie alongside the grid; stop as soon as the current prefix isn't in the trie.

title: Unique Paths III
statement: A robot cleans a floor plan grid: 1 is the start tile, 2 is the end tile, 0 is a dirty tile and -1 is a wall. The robot moves up, down, left or right. Count the routes from start to end that step on every non-wall tile exactly once. Return that count.
constraints: 1 ≤ rows·cols ≤ 20, exactly one start and one end
hint: Count the tiles you must visit, then DFS from the start, marking tiles visited; a route counts only if you reach the end after visiting all of them.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
statement: On an old phone keypad, 2=abc, 3=def, 4=ghi, 5=jkl, 6=mno, 7=pqrs, 8=tuv, 9=wxyz. Given a string digits of keys 2–9, return every letter string you could spell by choosing one letter per key, in key order. If digits is empty, return an empty list. Any order.
hint: Recurse position by position, appending each letter of the current key.

title: All Possible Full Binary Trees
statement: A full binary tree is one where every node has either 0 or 2 children. List every differently-shaped full binary tree with exactly n nodes. Describe each shape as a preorder string: visit the node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree, writing x for a node with two children and o for a leaf. For example, a root with two leaf children is "xoo". Return all shapes in any order (an empty list if none exist).
hint: A full tree with n nodes is a root plus a left full tree of i nodes and a right one of n−1−i nodes (i odd). Build recursively and memoize by n.

title: Expression Add Operators
statement: Given a digit string num and an integer target, insert +, - or * between some of the digits (digits may also be glued together into multi-digit numbers) so the expression evaluates to target with normal precedence (* before +/-). Numbers may not have leading zeros (a lone 0 is fine). Return every such expression in any order.
hint: Backtrack over where the next number ends, carrying the running value and the last multiplied term so '*' can undo it: val − last + last·cur.

title: Word Break II
statement: A message s lost all its spaces. Given a vocabulary words (each word may be used any number of times), return every way to insert spaces into s so that each resulting piece is a vocabulary word. Each answer is the pieces joined by single spaces. Return them in any order (an empty list if impossible).
constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 20, 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 1000, words are distinct, lowercase letters, at most 10<sup>5</sup> answers
hint: Backtrack from each index trying every vocabulary word that matches there; memoize the list of sentences for each suffix start.

title: 01 Matrix
statement: You get a grid of 0s and 1s containing at least one 0. Build a grid of the same size where each cell holds the number of up/down/left/right steps from that cell to the closest 0. Cells that are already 0 hold 0.
constraints: 1 ≤ rows, cols ≤ 300; at least one cell is 0
hint: Run one BFS that starts from every 0 at the same time; the first time a cell is reached gives its distance.

title: Clone Graph
statement:
An undirected graph has nodes 0..n-1; adj[v] lists the neighbours of v. Make a copy of the part of the graph reachable from start, giving copied nodes new labels 0, 1, 2, … in the order a BFS discovers them (the BFS starts at start, which becomes 0, and explores each node's neighbours in increasing original label).

Return the copy's adjacency list: row i holds the new labels of copy-node i's neighbours, sorted ascending.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>; total edges ≤ 2·10<sup>4</sup>; no self-loops or duplicate edges; 0 ≤ start < n
hint: BFS from start with a map old→new label; assign a new label when a node is first seen, then translate every edge through the map.

title: Rotting Oranges
statement: A rack is a grid where 0 is an empty slot, 1 a fresh loaf and 2 a mouldy loaf. Every minute, mould spreads from each mouldy loaf to fresh loaves directly above, below, left or right of it. Return the minutes until no fresh loaf is left, or -1 if some loaf can never be reached.
hint: Multi-source BFS from all mouldy loaves; count BFS layers and check whether any fresh loaf remains.

title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
statement: In an n × n grid, 0 is open and 1 is a wall. You may step to any of the 8 surrounding cells (including diagonals) if it is open. Return the number of cells on the shortest path from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell (both included), or -1 if no path exists.
hint: Plain BFS over cells with 8 directions; the first time you pop the target, its distance is the answer.

title: Word Ladder
statement:
Starting from begin, you may change exactly one letter at a time, and every word you pass through (except begin) must appear in words. Return how many words the shortest such chain from begin to end contains, counting both ends, or 0 if end cannot be reached.

Example idea: abc → abd → add is a chain of 3 words.
constraints: 1 ≤ word length ≤ 10; all words have the same length and are lowercase; 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 5000; begin ≠ end
hint: BFS where each word is a node; generate neighbours by trying every letter at every position and keeping those in the word set.

title: Flood Fill
statement: A picture is a grid of colour numbers. Using a paint bucket on cell (row, col) recolours that cell and every cell connected to it (up/down/left/right) through cells of the same original colour to color. Return the picture after the fill.
hint: DFS (with an explicit stack) from the start cell, visiting only neighbours that still have the original colour. If the new colour equals the old one, nothing changes.

title: Number of Islands
statement: A map is a grid of '1' (land) and '0' (sea). Land cells touching up/down/left/right belong to the same land mass. Return the number of separate land masses.
hint: Scan the grid; each time you find unvisited land, count it and sink its whole land mass with DFS/BFS.

title: All Paths from Source to Target
statement: A directed acyclic graph has nodes 0..n-1; graph[v] lists the nodes you can go to from v. Return every path that starts at node 0 and ends at node n-1, each path as the list of nodes visited. The paths may be returned in any order.
constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 14; the graph has no cycles
hint: Backtracking DFS from 0 keeping the current path; record a copy whenever you reach n-1.

title: Find Eventual Safe States
statement: A directed graph has nodes 0..n-1; graph[v] lists where you can go from v. A node is safe if every possible walk from it ends at a node with no outgoing edges (so no walk can loop forever). Return all safe nodes in increasing order.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>; total edges ≤ 4·10<sup>4</sup>; self-loops may appear
hint: Colour nodes white/grey/black in a DFS: a node is unsafe if it reaches a grey node (a cycle) or an unsafe node. Or reverse edges and peel off nodes with out-degree 0.

title: Count Provinces
statement: There are n students. friends[i][j] = 1 means students i and j are direct friends (the matrix is symmetric and friends[i][i] = 1). Friendship spreads: friends of friends are in the same circle. Return the number of circles.
hint: Count connected components: DFS/BFS from each unvisited student, or union-find over all 1 entries.

title: Surrounded Regions
statement: A board holds 'X' and 'O' cells. A group of 'O's (connected up/down/left/right) is trapped if none of its cells lies on the border of the board. Turn every trapped 'O' into 'X', modifying board in place. Your function returns nothing; we check board afterwards.
hint: Flip the logic: DFS from every border 'O' to mark the safe ones, then convert every unmarked 'O'.

title: Is Graph Bipartite
statement: Nodes 0..n-1 form an undirected graph; graph[v] lists the neighbours of v. Can every node be put on one of two teams so that each edge joins nodes on different teams? Return true or false. The graph may be disconnected.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>; total edges ≤ 3·10<sup>4</sup>; no self-loops or duplicate edges
hint: Colour each component with DFS/BFS alternating 0/1; a neighbour with the same colour means it's impossible.

title: Max Area of Island
statement: A map grid has 1 for land and 0 for water. Land cells touching up/down/left/right form one land mass, and its area is its number of cells. Return the largest area, or 0 if there is no land.
hint: DFS each unvisited land cell, counting cells as you visit them; keep the maximum.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
statement: A grid gives land heights. The west sea touches the top and left edges; the east sea touches the bottom and right edges. Rain flows from a cell to a neighbour (up/down/left/right) whose height is less than or equal to its own, and from edge cells into the adjacent sea. Return the [row, col] of every cell whose rain can reach both seas, in any order.
hint: Search uphill from each sea's edge cells to find what drains into it, then intersect the two reachable sets.

title: Critical Connections in a Network
statement: A connected network has servers 0..n-1 and undirected cables links[i] = [a, b]. A cable is critical if removing it splits the network into pieces. Return all critical cables, each as a pair, in any order (the order of the pair and of the list does not matter).
constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>; n−1 ≤ links.length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>; no duplicate cables or self-loops
hint: Tarjan's bridge finding: DFS with discovery times and low-links; edge (v,u) is a bridge when low[u] > disc[v].

title: Course Schedule
statement: There are n training modules numbered 0..n-1. Each pair [a, b] in needs means module b must be completed before module a. Return true if some order lets you complete all modules, otherwise false.
hint: It's possible exactly when the dependency graph has no cycle: run Kahn's algorithm and check that every module gets processed.

title: Course Schedule II
statement: Modules 0..n-1 have prerequisites: [a, b] in needs means b must be done before a. Return an order that completes every module. If several orders work, return the lexicographically smallest one (at each step take the smallest-numbered module that is available). Return an empty list if no order exists.
hint: Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap instead of a plain queue gives the smallest valid order.

title: Alien Dictionary
statement: A language uses lowercase English letters in an unknown order. words is a list of words claimed to be sorted by that order (as in a dictionary: a word comes before any longer word it is a prefix of). Return a string of all distinct letters that appear, in an order consistent with the list. If many orders are consistent, return the one that is smallest in normal alphabetical comparison (always pick the alphabetically smallest available letter). If the list cannot be sorted under any order, return "".
hint: Compare each adjacent pair: the first differing letters give an edge. A longer word before its own prefix is invalid. Then Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap.

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
statement: Each ticket [from, to] is a one-way flight between airport codes. Starting at airport start, plan a trip that uses every ticket exactly once. At least one such trip is guaranteed. If several exist, return the one whose list of airports is smallest when compared code by code alphabetically. Return the airports in the order visited.
hint: Hierholzer's algorithm: sort each airport's destinations, DFS greedily taking the smallest unused ticket, and add airports to the answer when you get stuck; reverse at the end.

title: Redundant Connection
statement: A network of n nodes labelled 1..n was a tree, then one extra undirected cable was added. edges lists all n cables. Return the cable you could delete to get a tree back; if several cables work, return the one that appears last in edges.
hint: Union-find: add cables in order; the first cable whose two ends are already connected closes the cycle and is the answer.

title: Connecting Cities (Min Cost)
statement: Lamp posts stand at integer points points[i] = [x, y]. A wire between two posts costs their Manhattan distance |x1−x2| + |y1−y2|. Return the minimum total cost so that every post is connected to every other (directly or through other posts).
constraints: 1 ≤ points.length ≤ 1000; all points distinct; −1000 ≤ x, y ≤ 1000
hint: It's a minimum spanning tree on a complete graph: O(n²) Prim's works well, or Kruskal on all pairs.

title: Accounts Merge
statement: Each card is [name, email1, email2, …]. Two cards belong to the same person if they share at least one email (directly or through a chain of cards). Cards sharing a name but no email may be different people. Merge them and return one list per person: the name first, then all of that person's distinct emails sorted alphabetically. The people may be listed in any order.
constraints: 1 ≤ cards.length ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>; each card has 1–10 emails; at most 5·10<sup>4</sup> distinct emails
hint: Union-find over emails (union every email on a card with the card's first email), then group emails by root.

title: Network Delay Time
statement: Nodes are labelled 1..n. Each times[i] = [u, v, w] is a one-way link: a signal sent from u arrives at v after w time units. A signal starts at node k. Return the time when the last node receives it, or -1 if some node never does.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>; 0 ≤ times.length ≤ 5·10<sup>4</sup>; 0 ≤ w ≤ 100; no duplicate (u, v) pairs
hint: Dijkstra from k; the answer is the largest finite distance, or -1 if any node stays unreached.

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
statement: Cities are numbered 0..n-1. Each flights[i] = [from, to, price] is a one-way flight. Return the cheapest total price to travel from src to dst using at most k intermediate stops (so at most k+1 flights), or -1 if it can't be done.
constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 100; 1 ≤ price ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>; 0 ≤ k < n; src ≠ dst; no duplicate flights
hint: Bellman–Ford limited to k+1 rounds, copying the distance array each round so a round only uses one more flight.

title: Swim in Rising Water
statement: An n × n grid holds distinct heights 0..n²−1. At time t the water level is t, and you can stand on any cell with height ≤ t and move instantly between such cells sharing an edge. Return the earliest time at which you can get from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 300; heights are a permutation of 0..n²−1
hint: Dijkstra / min-heap where a path's cost is the largest height on it; pop cells in order of that cost until you reach the corner.

title: Path With Minimum Effort
statement: A grid gives terrain heights. You walk from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, moving up/down/left/right. A route's strain is the largest absolute height difference between two consecutive cells on it. Return the smallest possible strain.
hint: Dijkstra where a path's cost is its maximum step, not its sum; or binary search the strain and check reachability with BFS.

title: Find the City With Smallest Neighbors
statement: Towns 0..n-1 are joined by two-way roads roads[i] = [a, b, length]. For each town, count how many other towns can be reached by a route of total length at most limit. Return the town with the smallest count; if several tie, return the one with the largest number.
hint: All-pairs shortest paths with Floyd–Warshall (n is small), then count per town.

title: Merge Intervals
statement:
A meeting room's bookings are given as slots, each [start, end], in no particular order. Bookings that overlap or touch (share an endpoint) should be fused into one block.

Return the fused blocks sorted by start time.
hint: Sort by start. Walk the list and either extend the last block (if the next start ≤ its end) or open a new block.

title: Insert Interval
statement:
booked is a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start. Add the interval extra to it, fusing it with any interval it overlaps or touches.

Return the resulting list, still sorted and non-overlapping.
hint: Copy every interval that ends before extra starts, absorb all that overlap into extra, then copy the rest.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
statement:
A single stage has show requests shows[i] = [start, end]. Two shows clash if one starts before the other ends; a show may start exactly when another ends.

Return the minimum number of shows to cancel so that no two remaining shows clash.
hint: Sort by end time and greedily keep every show that starts at or after the last kept end. Everything else is cancelled.

title: Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons
statement:
Targets hang along a line; target i spans [left, right] on the x-axis. A vertical laser fired at position x destroys every target with left ≤ x ≤ right.

Return the minimum number of shots needed to destroy all targets.
hint: Sort by right end. Fire at the right end of the first undestroyed target; it takes out every target starting at or before that point.

title: Jump Game
statement:
A frog sits on stone 0 of a row. From stone i it can hop forward to any stone up to stones[i] positions ahead.

Return true if the frog can reach the last stone, otherwise false.
hint: Track the farthest reachable index while scanning. If you ever stand past it, you're stuck.

title: Jump Game II
statement:
Same row of stones: from stone i the frog may hop forward up to stones[i] positions. The last stone is always reachable.

Return the minimum number of hops needed to get from stone 0 to the last stone.
hint: Think in BFS layers: all stones reachable with k hops form a window; the next window ends at the farthest reach from inside the current one.

title: Car Pooling
statement:
A shuttle drives only forward along a road and has seats seats. Each booking rides[i] = [people, from, to] means that many people board at kilometre from and leave at kilometre to (they free their seats at to, before anyone boards there).

Return true if every booking can be served without ever exceeding the seat count.
hint: Record +people at each pick-up and −people at each drop-off (a difference array), then sweep and check the running sum.

title: Min Taps to Water Garden
statement:
A lawn stretches from point 0 to point n. There is a sprinkler at every integer point i (0 ≤ i ≤ n); when switched on it waters [i − reach[i], i + reach[i]].

Return the minimum number of sprinklers to switch on so the whole lawn [0, n] is watered, or -1 if that is impossible.
hint: For each left point store the farthest right end any sprinkler reaches from there; then it's the fewest-hops greedy over the line.

title: Maximum Units on a Truck
statement:
A warehouse has crate types crates[i] = [count, itemsPerCrate]. A van can carry at most capacity crates (of any types).

Return the maximum total number of items the van can carry.
hint: Load crates with the most items per crate first until the van is full.

title: Assign Cookies
statement:
Kid i is happy only with a snack of size at least need[i]. You have snacks of sizes sizes; each kid gets at most one snack and each snack goes to at most one kid.

Return the maximum number of happy kids.
hint: Sort both. Give each kid (smallest need first) the smallest snack that still satisfies them.

title: Lemonade Change
statement:
A ticket costs 5 coins. Customers arrive in order and each pays with a single note of 5, 10 or 20 (notes[i]). The booth starts with no money and must give exact change using only notes it has received.

Return true if every customer can be given correct change.
hint: Count 5s and 10s. For a 20, prefer giving 10+5 over 5+5+5 to keep small notes.

title: Largest Number
statement:
Given non-negative integers nums, arrange them in some order and glue their digits together to form the largest possible number.

Return it as a string (with no leading zeros, so all zeros give "0").
hint: Put a before b when a+b (as strings) is larger than b+a.

title: Partition Labels
statement:
Cut the lowercase string s into as many consecutive chunks as possible so that each letter appears in at most one chunk.

Return the lengths of the chunks from left to right.
hint: Record each letter's last index. Extend the current chunk's end to the last index of every letter you see; cut when you reach that end.

title: Next Permutation
statement:
Rearrange nums in place into the next arrangement in lexicographic (dictionary) order. If nums is already the largest arrangement, rearrange it into the smallest one (ascending).

Your function returns nothing; we check nums afterwards. Use only O(1) extra memory.
hint: Find the rightmost i with nums[i] < nums[i+1], swap it with the rightmost larger element after it, then reverse the suffix after i.

title: Gas Station
statement:
An electric scooter rides a circular route of charging points. At point i it gains charge[i] units, and riding from point i to point i+1 (wrapping around) uses drain[i] units. The battery starts empty and must never go negative.

Return the smallest starting index from which the scooter can complete one full loop, or -1 if no start works.
hint: If total charge < total drain, answer −1. Otherwise scan once, resetting the start whenever the running balance goes negative. (Several starts can work when totals are equal; return the smallest.)

title: Candy Distribution
statement:
Children stand in a line with scores scores. Give each child at least one sticker, and any child with a strictly higher score than an immediate neighbour must get more stickers than that neighbour.

Return the minimum total number of stickers.
hint: Two passes: left-to-right fixes the left-neighbour rule, right-to-left fixes the right-neighbour rule; take the max of both at each child.

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
statement:
Each rung i of a ladder charges a toll toll[i] when you step on it. You may start on rung 0 or rung 1, and from any rung you may climb 1 or 2 rungs. The top is just past the last rung.

Return the minimum total toll to reach the top.
hint: best[i] = toll[i] + min(best[i−1], best[i−2]); answer is min of the last two.

title: Decode Ways
statement:
Letters are encoded as numbers: A→1, B→2, …, Z→26. A message was encoded and the numbers written back to back, giving the digit string code.

Return how many different letter messages could produce code. Pieces may not have a leading zero (so "05" is not a valid piece).
hint: ways[i] = ways[i−1] if the last digit is 1–9, plus ways[i−2] if the last two digits form 10–26.

title: House Robber II
statement:
Market stalls stand in a circle; stall i offers coins[i] coins. You may collect from any set of stalls as long as no two chosen stalls are adjacent (the first and last stalls are adjacent too).

Return the maximum number of coins you can collect.
hint: The first and last can't both be chosen: solve the straight-line version on coins[0..n−2] and on coins[1..n−1], take the max.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement:
Pick some elements of nums (keeping their original order) so that each picked value is strictly larger than the one before it.

Return the largest number of elements you can pick.
hint: O(n²): best[i] = 1 + max best[j] for j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]. O(n log n): keep the smallest tail for each length and binary-search.

title: Perfect Squares
statement:
Write the positive integer n as a sum of perfect squares (1, 4, 9, 16, …), repeats allowed.

Return the smallest number of squares needed.
hint: best[x] = 1 + min over squares s ≤ x of best[x − s].

title: Unique Paths II
statement:
A robot starts at the top-left cell of grid and wants to reach the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down. Cells with 1 are walls the robot cannot enter; 0 cells are open.

Return the number of distinct routes (0 if the start or end is a wall).
hint: ways[r][c] = ways[r−1][c] + ways[r][c−1] for open cells, 0 for walls.

title: Minimum Path Sum
statement:
Each cell of grid holds a non-negative cost. Walk from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell moving only right or down, paying the cost of every cell you visit (including both ends).

Return the minimum total cost.
hint: cost[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(cost from above, cost from the left).

title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
statement:
Drop a marble onto any cell of the first row of the square grid grid. From cell (r, c) it falls to row r+1 in column c−1, c or c+1 (staying inside the grid), until it leaves the last row.

Return the minimum possible sum of the cells it passes through.
hint: Row by row: best[c] = grid[r][c] + min of best in columns c−1, c, c+1 of the previous row.

title: Dungeon Game
statement:
An explorer enters a cave at the top-left cell of cave and must reach the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down. Each cell changes stamina by cave[r][c] (negative drains, positive restores), including the first and last cells. If stamina ever drops to 0 or below, the explorer collapses.

Return the minimum starting stamina (at least 1) needed to reach the exit.
hint: Work backwards from the exit: need[r][c] = max(1, min(need right, need below) − cave[r][c]).

title: Cherry Pickup
statement:
In the square field field, a cell is 1 (a berry), 0 (empty) or -1 (a rock you can't pass). Walk from the top-left to the bottom-right moving only right/down, then return to the top-left moving only left/up. Every berry you step on is picked once (the cell becomes empty).

Return the maximum number of berries you can pick, or 0 if the bottom-right can't be reached.
hint: Treat the return trip as a second walker going forward at the same time. With both walkers on step k, state (k, r1, r2) is enough; count a shared cell once.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement:
Two strings a and b are given. A trail is a string you can get from both of them by deleting some characters (possibly none) without reordering the rest.

Return the length of the longest trail they share. For example, "plane" and "apple" share "ple", length 3.
hint: dp[i][j] = answer for prefixes a[:i], b[:j]. If a[i-1]==b[j-1] take dp[i-1][j-1]+1, else the max of dropping one character.

title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
statement:
Given a string s, delete any characters you like (keeping the order of the rest) so that what remains reads the same forwards and backwards.

Return the maximum possible length of what remains. For example, "character" contains "carac", length 5.
hint: dp[i][j] for substring s[i..j]: if the ends match, 2 + dp[i+1][j-1]; otherwise max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

title: Edit Distance
statement:
You want to turn the string src into the string dst. In one step you may insert one character, delete one character, or overwrite one character with another.

Return the minimum number of steps needed. For example, "kitten" becomes "sitting" in 3 steps.
hint: dp[i][j] = cost for prefixes. Equal last chars cost dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise 1 + min(insert, delete, replace).

title: Shortest Common Supersequence
statement:
Find the shortest string that contains both a and b as subsequences (each can be obtained from it by deleting characters without reordering).

Return the length of that shortest string. For example, for "bake" and "cake" the string "bcake" works, so the answer is 5.
hint: Characters in the longest common subsequence can be shared, so the answer is len(a) + len(b) − LCS(a, b). (To build the string itself, walk the LCS table backwards.)

title: Minimum Insertions to Make Palindrome
statement:
You may insert any character at any position of s, as many times as you like.

Return the minimum number of insertions needed to make s read the same forwards and backwards. For example, "abb" needs one insertion ("abba").
hint: Characters already in the longest palindromic subsequence can stay; every other character needs a partner. Answer = n − LPS(s). Or dp on intervals directly.

title: Regular Expression Matching
statement:
Decide whether the pattern p matches the whole text t. In the pattern:

  • a letter matches that same letter,
  • . matches any single character,
  • * means zero or more copies of the character just before it (a letter or .).

Return true if it matches. For example, "x*y." matches "xxyz".
constraints: 0 ≤ t.length ≤ 40, 0 ≤ p.length ≤ 40; every * follows a letter or a dot
hint: dp[i][j] = t[i:] matches p[j:]. If p[j+1] is '*', either skip the pair (dp[i][j+2]) or consume one char if it matches (dp[i+1][j]).

title: Distinct Subsequences
statement:
Count in how many different ways the string word can be picked out of text as a subsequence: choose positions in text, in increasing order, whose characters spell word. Two ways differ if their chosen position sets differ.

Return the count (it fits in a 64-bit integer). For example, "ab" can be picked out of "aabb" in 4 ways: either a paired with either b.
constraints: 0 ≤ text.length ≤ 300, 0 ≤ word.length ≤ 6, lowercase letters; the answer is < 2<sup>53</sup>
hint: dp[j] = ways to form word[:j] so far. Scan text; for each char, update j from right to left: if text[i]==word[j-1], dp[j] += dp[j-1].

title: Palindrome Partitioning II
statement:
Cut the string s into consecutive pieces so that every piece reads the same forwards and backwards.

Return the minimum number of cuts needed. For example, "noonabc" needs 3 cuts: noon|a|b|c.
hint: Expand around every center to mark palindromes s[l..r]; then cuts[r] = min over such l of cuts[l-1] + 1 (0 if l == 0).

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
statement:
You have items with positive weights w. Every item must go into one of two bags.

Return true if the items can be split so both bags weigh exactly the same. For example, [2, 3, 4, 5] splits as {2, 5} and {3, 4}.
hint: If the total is odd, no. Otherwise run a 0/1 knapsack reachability on sum/2, iterating capacity downwards.

title: Coin Change
statement:
A machine accepts tokens of the values in tokens; you have unlimited tokens of each value. Pay exactly fare.

Return the fewest tokens needed, or -1 if the exact fare can't be paid. A fare of 0 needs 0 tokens.
hint: best[a] = 1 + min over token t of best[a − t]; fill a from 1 to fare.

title: Coin Change II
statement:
Using unlimited tokens of the distinct values in tokens, count how many different combinations pay exactly fare. Order doesn't matter: 1+2 and 2+1 are the same combination.

Return the count (it fits in a 64-bit integer). Paying 0 has exactly 1 way (use nothing).
constraints: 1 ≤ tokens.length ≤ 10, 1 ≤ tokens[i] ≤ 100, values distinct, 0 ≤ fare ≤ 1000; answer < 2<sup>53</sup>
hint: Loop over token values in the outer loop and amounts in the inner loop: ways[a] += ways[a − t]. That order counts combinations, not orderings.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
statement:
prices[i] is the price of one share on day i. You may hold at most one share at a time, and can buy and sell as many times as you like (you may even sell and buy again on the same day).

Return the maximum total profit.
hint: Track two states per day: holding vs not holding. Equivalently, add every positive day-to-day increase.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
statement:
prices[i] is a share's price on day i. Hold at most one share at a time and trade as often as you like, but after you sell you must rest for one full day before buying again.

Return the maximum total profit.
hint: Three states: holding, just sold (resting tomorrow), free. hold = max(hold, free − p); sold = hold + p; free = max(free, previous sold).

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Fee
statement:
prices[i] is a share's price on day i. Hold at most one share at a time and trade as often as you like, but every completed buy-then-sell round trip costs a broker fee of fee.

Return the maximum total profit after fees.
hint: Holding/free states again; subtract the fee when you sell: free = max(free, hold + p − fee).

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
statement:
prices[i] is a share's price on day i. You may complete at most two buy-then-sell round trips, holding at most one share at a time (sell before buying again).

Return the maximum total profit.
hint: Keep four running values: best after first buy, first sell, second buy, second sell, updating them in that order each day.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
statement:
You may complete at most k buy-then-sell round trips on the daily prices prices, holding at most one share at a time.

Return the maximum total profit.
hint: For each j = 1..k keep buy[j] and sell[j]: buy[j] = max(buy[j], sell[j−1] − p), sell[j] = max(sell[j], buy[j] + p).

title: Burst Balloons
statement:
A row of lanterns has brightness values vals. Popping lantern i earns left × vals[i] × right, where left and right are the brightness of its current nearest unpopped neighbours (use 1 if there is no neighbour on that side). The row then closes the gap.

Pop every lantern in the best order and return the maximum total earned.
hint: Pad with 1 on both ends. dp[l][r] = best for lanterns strictly between l and r; try each k as the LAST one popped there: dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + v[l]·v[k]·v[r].

title: Minimum Cost to Merge Stones
statement:
Sand piles stand in a row with sizes piles. One move fuses exactly k adjacent piles into a single pile, costing the total sand in those k piles.

Return the minimum total cost to end with one pile, or -1 if that is impossible. (Already one pile costs 0.)
hint: Possible only if (n − 1) % (k − 1) == 0. dp[i][j] = min cost to squeeze piles i..j as far as possible; split at m stepping by k−1, and add sum(i..j) when (j − i) % (k − 1) == 0.

title: Min Cost to Cut a Stick
statement:
A plank runs from position 0 to length. You must saw it at every position listed in marks (distinct, strictly between 0 and length), in any order you choose. Each saw cut costs the length of the piece being cut at that moment.

Return the minimum total cost of making all the cuts.
hint: Sort marks and add 0 and length. dp[i][j] = cheapest way to make all cuts strictly between points i and j = (p[j] − p[i]) + min over m of dp[i][m] + dp[m][j].

title: House Robber III
statement:
An orchard is shaped like a binary tree; each node's value is the fruit on that tree. You may harvest any set of nodes, but never two nodes that are directly connected (a parent and its child).

Return the most fruit you can harvest. The tree is given in level order with null for missing children.
hint: Post-order DFS returning a pair (best if this node is taken, best if skipped). take = val + skip(left) + skip(right); skip = max of each child's pair, summed.

title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
statement:
Build a class PrefixTree that stores lowercase words. insert(word) adds a word, search(word) returns true only if that exact word was inserted, and startsWith(prefix) returns true if any inserted word begins with prefix.

Line 1 lists the operations, line 2 their arguments; the output holds each call's return value (null for calls that return nothing).
constraints: 1 ≤ word.length, prefix.length ≤ 2000, lowercase letters only; at most 3·10<sup>4</sup> calls.
hint: Each node keeps up to 26 children plus an end-of-word flag. Walk character by character; search also checks the flag at the end.

title: Add and Search Word
statement:
Build a class PatternDictionary. addWord(word) stores a lowercase word. search(pattern) returns true if some stored word has the same length as pattern and matches it, where a . in the pattern matches any single letter.

Line 1 lists the operations, line 2 their arguments; the output holds each call's return value (null for void calls).
constraints: 1 ≤ word.length ≤ 25; patterns contain lowercase letters and at most 2 dots; at most 2·10<sup>4</sup> calls.
hint: Store words in a trie. On a dot, try every child recursively; on a letter, follow just that child.

title: Longest Common Prefix
statement: Given a list of strings words, return the longest string that every word begins with. If the words share no starting letter, return an empty string.
hint: Insert the words into a trie (or compare column by column) and walk down while there is exactly one child and no word ends there.

title: Search Suggestions System
statement:
A search box knows the names in products. The user types query one letter at a time. After each letter, list up to three product names that start with what has been typed so far, choosing the alphabetically smallest ones.

Return one list per typed letter (an empty list when nothing matches).
constraints: 1 ≤ products.length ≤ 5·10<sup>4</sup>, products are distinct lowercase strings, 1 ≤ query.length ≤ 1000.
hint: Sort the products; for each prefix binary-search the first name ≥ prefix and take up to three that still start with it (or use a trie keeping the 3 smallest at each node).

title: Word Break
statement:
Return true if the string text can be cut into pieces so that every piece appears in dict. A dictionary word may be used any number of times.

For instance, "redbluered" with ["red","blue"] works.
constraints: 1 ≤ text.length ≤ 300, 1 ≤ dict.length ≤ 1000, 1 ≤ dict[i].length ≤ 20, all distinct lowercase.
hint: ok[i] = text[:i] can be split. ok[i] is true if some ok[j] is true and text[j:i] is a dictionary word (walk a trie from j to find all such i).

title: Replace Words
statement: You get a list of short roots and a sentence of lowercase words separated by single spaces. Replace every word that begins with some root by the shortest such root; leave other words unchanged. Return the new sentence.
hint: Put the roots in a trie. For each word, walk the trie and stop at the first node marked as the end of a root.

title: Concatenated Words
statement: Given a list of distinct lowercase words, return every word that can be written as two or more shorter words from the same list joined together (pieces may repeat). Return them in any order.
constraints: 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 10<sup>4</sup>, 1 ≤ words[i].length ≤ 30, total length ≤ 10<sup>5</sup>, all words distinct.
hint: Sort by length. For each word run a word-break check against the words already seen (all shorter), then add it to the set/trie.

title: Sum of All Subset XOR Totals
statement:
For every subset of nums (including the empty one, whose XOR is 0), compute the XOR of its elements. Return the sum of all these XOR values.

For [2,3] the subsets give 0, 2, 3 and 1, so the answer is 6.
hint: Enumerate subsets with recursion or bitmasks. (Shortcut: each bit set anywhere contributes in exactly half the subsets, so the answer is (OR of all) · 2<sup>n−1</sup>.)

title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in Array
statement: Given non-negative integers nums, return the largest value of nums[i] XOR nums[j] over all pairs with 0 ≤ i ≤ j < n (so a single element gives 0).
hint: Insert numbers bit by bit (high to low) into a binary trie. For each number, greedily walk toward the opposite bit whenever that child exists.

title: Maximum XOR With an Element From Array
statement:
You get non-negative integers nums and a list of queries, each [x, cap]. For a query, consider only elements of nums that are ≤ cap; return the largest x XOR element among them, or -1 if no element qualifies.

Return the answers in query order.
hint: Answer queries offline: sort queries by cap and nums ascending, insert numbers ≤ cap into a binary trie, then greedily take the opposite bit.

title: Missing Number
statement: The array nums holds n distinct numbers taken from 0, 1, …, n, so exactly one value from that range is absent. Return it.
hint: XOR all indices 0..n together with all values; every present number cancels, leaving the missing one.

title: Number of 1 Bits
statement:
Given a non-negative integer n, return how many 1s appear in its binary representation.

For example 13 is 1101 in binary, which has three ones.
hint: Repeatedly do n &= n − 1, which clears the lowest set bit; count how many times until n is 0.

title: Power of Two
statement: Return true if the integer n equals 2k for some integer k ≥ 0, otherwise false. Note that zero and negative numbers are never powers of two.
hint: A positive power of two has exactly one set bit, so n > 0 and n & (n − 1) == 0.

title: Single Number
statement: In nums every value appears exactly twice except one, which appears once. Return that lonely value using O(1) extra space.
hint: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so XOR-ing everything leaves the unpaired value.

title: Single Number II
statement: Every value in nums appears exactly three times, except one value that appears once. Return that value in linear time and constant extra space.
hint: For each of the 32 bit positions, count how many numbers have it set; counts not divisible by 3 belong to the single value (handle the sign bit for negatives).

title: Single Number III
statement: In nums exactly two distinct values appear once and every other value appears exactly twice. Return those two values as [smaller, larger].
hint: XOR everything to get a ^ b. Pick any set bit of it (e.g. x & −x) and split the numbers into two groups by that bit; XOR each group.

title: XOR Queries of a Subarray
statement: You get an array arr of non-negative integers and queries, each [left, right] (0-based, inclusive). For every query return the XOR of arr[left..right], in query order.
hint: Build prefix XORs p where p[i+1] = p[i] ^ arr[i]; the answer for [l, r] is p[r+1] ^ p[l].
